blocks.text: Level Up Your ChatGPT Skills

Most people who reach this course use ChatGPT every day — for drafts, research, summaries, and quick answers.

The basics aren't the problem. The gap is between daily use and real leverage. That's what this course covers — the moves that turn a capable user into one who consistently gets better results on complex, professional work.

Ready? Let's start!
Custom GPTs Built for Multi-Step Workflows

You've likely seen Custom GPTs in ChatGPT before — a version of ChatGPT you set up with specific instructions so it can work like a specialized assistant — or even built one yourself. The next move is to push this knowledge forward. 

This lesson guides you through the cases when the input is missing, contradictory, or wildly off-scope. You'll see what already exists in the GPT Store, learn when it fits and when it doesn't, and then build a GPT that holds up under messy inputs and multi-step workflows.
Where Custom GPTs Earn Their Keep

Custom GPTs are worth building when you repeat the same type of task every month, week, or even more often — like meal planning, budget reviews, client onboarding, or preparing lessons for the same students.
You have two paths:

• Discover a Custom GPT someone else built
  • Build one for your specific case
This lesson does both.
Scenario: Managing Multiple Students

Mira is a chess coach with 12 students. She teaches in person on weekday afternoons and online through Chess.com in the evenings. All 12 are spread across the week, all at different ratings, all working on different parts of their game. Every Sunday, she prepares for the week ahead, which requires a lot of manual work: scheduling, planning, and lesson prep.
Four Students, Four Profiles
Mira's 12 students are a mixed group. Some of them are:

• Emma — beginner, learning basic tactics
  • Jane — intermediate, working on tactical patterns
  • Daniel — intermediate, focusing on middlegame play
  • Elias — advanced, refining endgame technique
Every student has a different focus area, a different next lesson, a different stack of progress notes.
What Mira Needs Out
For each student, she produces three things every week:

• Schedule — who's on for the week, in person or online, what time
  • Progress notes — what they worked on last session, what stuck, what didn't
  • Lesson plans — warm-up, main concept, practice puzzles, a game position to analyze

12 students and three outputs per student = 36 artifacts per week. A standard ChatGPT session won't be the most convenient environment to keep everything organized. That's where a Custom GPT comes in.

feedbackCorrect.text: A useful Custom GPT for Mira keeps student context in its knowledge files, produces multiple output types, and surfaces contradictions in notes. Playing chess well isn't the job — preparing lessons reliably is.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Chess strength matters for Mira, not for the GPT — she's the coach. The GPT's job is structural: hold student context, produce the three artifacts, and catch contradictions she might miss while prepping 12 students in a single Sunday afternoon.

options.label: Flag when student notes contradict each other
Produce three different output types from the same input
Remember each student's level and current focus area across weeks
Know how to play chess at a high level

blocks.question: What would a Custom GPT need to handle for Mira's setup to save her time?

blocks.text: Discover Before You Build

Now that we've identified the capabilities a Custom GPT should have to best suit Mira's needs, let's find one for her. Before building anything, browse the GPT Store. Someone may have already shipped a tool that handles part of this work. Open Explore GPTs in the sidebar and look for one that matches the case.
Auditing the GPT Store
Mira first checks the GPT Store for something she can reuse:

• Lesson Planner can generate ready-made lessons, but only one at a time from a fresh prompt. It doesn't remember students or track progress.
  • GTD Daily Planner Assistant helps organize schedules and weekly tasks, but it's designed for one person's productivity system — not 12 chess students with different skill levels and goals.
Both GPTs are useful, but neither can manage Mira's full workflow across weeks. Her use case is too specific for a general Store GPT, so it's time to build a Custom GPT.
One heads-up: building works on the web version of ChatGPT, and requires a paid plan. The mobile app can run GPTs but not build them.
blocks.title: An Important Note

blocks.text: Building Mira's Coaching Assistant
In Explore GPTs, tap + Create to open the GPT builder. Open the Configure tab and fill in the following fields:

• Name and Description label the GPT so Mira recognizes it later.
  • Instructions are the core, where the role and routing rules live.
  • Conversation starters are optional shortcut prompts for launching a session.
  • Knowledge is where she uploads files to add to the student list and progress logs that the GPT can draw on.
  • Recommended Model sets the ChatGPT model it runs on.
The preview panel on the right shows the GPT taking shape as she fills each field.

blocks.text:
The prompt from the previous task is exactly how you write the instructions for Custom GPT: structured and detailed enough. These techniques work with any Custom GPT:
  • Rules instead of suggestions: "Pause and ask" beats "Try to clarify when possible."
  • Specific fields instead of vague wording: "If focus area is missing" beats "If the request is vague."
  • One action per sentence: split "surface the contradiction and ask which wins" into two sentences. The GPT follows compound rules inconsistently.
blocks.title: 💡 How Strong Instructions Hold

blocks.text: It Works — Until It Doesn't

After setting up the instructions, Mira started using her Custom GPT. With a clean request like "Prep Daniel's Wednesday session; he's working on middlegame attacks," the GPT performs well, generating a solid lesson plan. But Mira's real Sunday-evening inputs are rarely that clean. They're often rushed, incomplete, and messy — and that's where Custom GPTs tend to break in four predictable ways.
Four Failure Modes

• Missing input: Required information isn't there.
  • Contradictory input: Two parts of the request fight each other.
  • Scope creep: Extra tasks slip in alongside the main one.
  • Scope underflow: The request is too vague to act on.
Without explicit routing for each, the GPT improvises. Silent improvisation is worse than failing visibly, as you don't know what went wrong until it's too late.

pairs.left: "Prep something for Jane tomorrow."
pairs.right: Missing input

pairs.left: "Make Daniel more aggressive in chess but more careful."
pairs.right: Contradictory input

pairs.left: "Lesson plan for Emma — also do one for her older brother who's visiting."
pairs.right: Scope creep

blocks.prompt: Match each of Mira's Sunday-night inputs to the failure mode it triggers.
blocks.title: Sort the Failure Modes

blocks.text: Routing for Missing Input

When a required field is missing, the GPT should ask for it. For Mira, "Prep something for Jane" leaves out focus area, session length, and format (in-person vs. online). The instruction needs to name the required fields and specify what to do when they're absent.

blocks.prompt: Complete the routing rule for missing required information.
blocks.template: If a required field is missing from the request — [field], format, or focus area  — [response action] before generating the artifact.

blocks.text: Routing for Contradictory Input

Great job! Now the GPT will ask for clarification when the input is incomplete. 

The next thing to consider is what to do when two parts of a request contradict each other, as you've seen in Daniel's case: "Make him more aggressive in chess but more careful." The GPT should surface the contradiction, not synthesize it away. 

Let's set up the rule for cases like this.

blocks.prompt: Complete the routing rule for contradictions inside the request.
blocks.template: If two parts of the request [conflict type] — like "more aggressive" and "more careful" — [command] and ask me to [resolution step]

blocks.text: Routing for Scope Creep and Underflow
Nicely done! The last two modes are opposites:

• Scope creep is when a side request smuggles itself into the main task — Emma's lesson plan with a tacked-on analysis of her brother's game. To fix it, prompt GPT to split the work and ask which to prioritize.
  • Scope underflow is when the request is too vague to act on — "same as last week for Elias" when last week covered three different things. To fix this one, prompt GPT to name what's missing and ask for one clarification.

The four-mode pattern is reusable for any Custom GPT, not just Mira's:
  • Missing input → name required fields, ask one question
  • Contradictory input → surface the conflict, ask which wins
  • Scope creep → split the work, confirm priority
  • Scope underflow → identify the missing specificity, narrow once
Wrap all four in the instructions, and the GPT stops improvising silently. It either produces what you asked for or asks before acting.
blocks.title: 💡 The Routing Pattern

feedbackCorrect.text: The missing-input clause names the required fields and forces a question. The GPT asks once, waits, then generates a lesson plan against Jane's actual focus for tomorrow.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Picking from past sessions or generating a generic plan is what the routing prevents. The clause exists so the GPT asks instead of guessing — that's the difference between a polished demo and a tool Mira can use at 9 p.m. on Sunday.

options.label: Picks the most likely focus area from past sessions
Asks which focus area before generating anything
Generates a generic lesson plan covering several focus areas

blocks.question: Mira sends "Prep something for Jane tomorrow." With the missing-input clause in place, what does the adjusted Custom GPT do?

blocks.text: The Full Sunday Run

Great job! With all the settings in place, Mira asks the GPT for a full-cycle next-week student prep. Her Custom GPT can now do that. Let's see how it handles the task. 

With the well-thought-out instructions, Mira's prompts can stay short. The GPT already knows everything it needs.

blocks.exampleResponse: Week of June 15 — 12 students scheduled — Monday in person — Emma (4 p.m.), 2 others — Tuesday online — Jane (5 p.m.), Daniel (7 p.m.) — Wednesday in person — Emma (4 p.m.), 1 other — Thursday online — Elias (8 p.m.), 3 others — Saturday in person — 1 catch-up Needs your input before I can finalize: — Jane's Tuesday focus area — last note mentions both tactical patterns and opening review — Daniel's session length — Wednesday block shows 60 min, last note says 90 — Elias — last three sessions covered different endgame types Ready to generate 9 lesson plans and 9 progress notes once you confirm the 3 pending items.
blocks.prompt: Mira asks her Custom GPT to prep the week. Complete the prompt that triggers a full weekly summary.
blocks.template: [Command] the week of [date]. List [session type] and online sessions separately by day.

blocks.text: The GPT That Holds
Mira's Custom GPT now does three things a Store GPT couldn't:

• Holds 12 students' states.
  • Produces three artifact types per student.
  • Routes around the four input failures that wreck a Sunday-evening prep session.
From now on, the same GPT handles all 36 artifacts.

• Custom GPTs earn their build cost when the task is structurally repetitive: Same shape, different input, every week.
  • Browse the GPT Store first: A general tool may already cover part of the work better than anything you'd build solo.
  • Build your own when the case is too specific for a general tool: Persistent state, multiple output types, custom rules.
  • Strong instructions are imperative: They name fields and contain one behavior per clause.
  • Four failure modes wreck most Custom GPTs: Missing input, contradictory input, scope creep, and scope underflow. Route around all four so the GPT doesn't improvise silently.
blocks.title: Key Takeaways

blocks.text: What's Next?

You've built a Custom GPT that holds up against messy inputs. The next lesson connects Custom GPTs to live data through Actions: the GPT can now read your calendar, write to your project tracker, and fetch from any API. Let's keep going!

After setting up the instructions, Mira started using her Custom GPT. With a clean request like "Prep Daniel's Wednesday session; he's working on middlegame attacks," the GPT performs well, generating a solid lesson plan. But Mira's real Sunday-evening inputs are rarely that clean. They're often rushed, incomplete, and messy — and that's where Custom GPTs tend to break in four predictable ways.
Four Failure Modes

• Missing input: Required information isn't there.
  • Contradictory input: Two parts of the request fight each other.
  • Scope creep: Extra tasks slip in alongside the main one.
  • Scope underflow: The request is too vague to act on.
Without explicit routing for each, the GPT improvises. Silent improvisation is worse than failing visibly, as you don't know what went wrong until it's too late.

pairs.left: "Prep something for Jane tomorrow."
pairs.right: Missing input

pairs.left: "Make Daniel more aggressive in chess but more careful."
pairs.right: Contradictory input

pairs.left: "Lesson plan for Emma — also do one for her older brother who's visiting."
pairs.right: Scope creep

blocks.prompt: Match each of Mira's Sunday-night inputs to the failure mode it triggers.
blocks.title: Sort the Failure Modes

blocks.text: Routing for Missing Input

When a required field is missing, the GPT should ask for it. For Mira, "Prep something for Jane" leaves out focus area, session length, and format (in-person vs. online). The instruction needs to name the required fields and specify what to do when they're absent.

blocks.prompt: Complete the routing rule for missing required information.
blocks.template: If a required field is missing from the request — [field], format, or focus area  — [response action] before generating the artifact.

blocks.text: Routing for Contradictory Input

Great job! Now the GPT will ask for clarification when the input is incomplete. 

The next thing to consider is what to do when two parts of a request contradict each other, as you've seen in Daniel's case: "Make him more aggressive in chess but more careful." The GPT should surface the contradiction, not synthesize it away. 

Let's set up the rule for cases like this.

blocks.prompt: Complete the routing rule for contradictions inside the request.
blocks.template: If two parts of the request [conflict type] — like "more aggressive" and "more careful" — [command] and ask me to [resolution step]

blocks.text: Routing for Scope Creep and Underflow
Nicely done! The last two modes are opposites:

• Scope creep is when a side request smuggles itself into the main task — Emma's lesson plan with a tacked-on analysis of her brother's game. To fix it, prompt GPT to split the work and ask which to prioritize.
  • Scope underflow is when the request is too vague to act on — "same as last week for Elias" when last week covered three different things. To fix this one, prompt GPT to name what's missing and ask for one clarification.

The four-mode pattern is reusable for any Custom GPT, not just Mira's:
  • Missing input → name required fields, ask one question
  • Contradictory input → surface the conflict, ask which wins
  • Scope creep → split the work, confirm priority
  • Scope underflow → identify the missing specificity, narrow once
Wrap all four in the instructions, and the GPT stops improvising silently. It either produces what you asked for or asks before acting.
blocks.title: 💡 The Routing Pattern

feedbackCorrect.text: The missing-input clause names the required fields and forces a question. The GPT asks once, waits, then generates a lesson plan against Jane's actual focus for tomorrow.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Picking from past sessions or generating a generic plan is what the routing prevents. The clause exists so the GPT asks instead of guessing — that's the difference between a polished demo and a tool Mira can use at 9 p.m. on Sunday.

options.label: Picks the most likely focus area from past sessions
Asks which focus area before generating anything
Generates a generic lesson plan covering several focus areas

blocks.question: Mira sends "Prep something for Jane tomorrow." With the missing-input clause in place, what does the adjusted Custom GPT do?

blocks.text: The Full Sunday Run

Great job! With all the settings in place, Mira asks the GPT for a full-cycle next-week student prep. Her Custom GPT can now do that. Let's see how it handles the task. 

With the well-thought-out instructions, Mira's prompts can stay short. The GPT already knows everything it needs.

blocks.exampleResponse: Week of June 15 — 12 students scheduled — Monday in person — Emma (4 p.m.), 2 others — Tuesday online — Jane (5 p.m.), Daniel (7 p.m.) — Wednesday in person — Emma (4 p.m.), 1 other — Thursday online — Elias (8 p.m.), 3 others — Saturday in person — 1 catch-up Needs your input before I can finalize: — Jane's Tuesday focus area — last note mentions both tactical patterns and opening review — Daniel's session length — Wednesday block shows 60 min, last note says 90 — Elias — last three sessions covered different endgame types Ready to generate 9 lesson plans and 9 progress notes once you confirm the 3 pending items.
blocks.prompt: Mira asks her Custom GPT to prep the week. Complete the prompt that triggers a full weekly summary.
blocks.template: [Command] the week of [date]. List [session type] and online sessions separately by day.

blocks.text: The GPT That Holds
Mira's Custom GPT now does three things a Store GPT couldn't:

• Holds 12 students' states.
  • Produces three artifact types per student.
  • Routes around the four input failures that wreck a Sunday-evening prep session.
From now on, the same GPT handles all 36 artifacts.

• Custom GPTs earn their build cost when the task is structurally repetitive: Same shape, different input, every week.
  • Browse the GPT Store first: A general tool may already cover part of the work better than anything you'd build solo.
  • Build your own when the case is too specific for a general tool: Persistent state, multiple output types, custom rules.
  • Strong instructions are imperative: They name fields and contain one behavior per clause.
  • Four failure modes wreck most Custom GPTs: Missing input, contradictory input, scope creep, and scope underflow. Route around all four so the GPT doesn't improvise silently.
blocks.title: Key Takeaways

blocks.text: What's Next?

You've built a Custom GPT that holds up against messy inputs. The next lesson connects Custom GPTs to live data through Actions: the GPT can now read your calendar, write to your project tracker, and fetch from any API. Let's keep going!

lessons.title: Custom GPT: Building for Multi-Step Workflows

blocks.text: Custom GPTs with Actions

In the previous lesson, you built Mira's coaching assistant. The Custom GPT holds 12 students' states and produces three different artifacts per student. Now it's time to add another layer.

Without live data, a Custom GPT can only work with what you've manually uploaded. To pull live data, like bank transactions, Custom GPTs require different settings. That's what this lesson covers.

Let's get started!
Mira's Other Sunday Problem

Lesson prep is solved. But every Sunday, Mira also sits down to check her finances — and that part still takes time.

End of June. It's time to check what came in, what went out, and plan for July.
Mira's money moves across multiple accounts and currencies. Her income looks like this:

• 8 kids on monthly subscriptions, paid by parents.
  • 4 adults paying per session, in USD, EUR, or GBP.
Her spending mixes personal and business: rent, groceries, Chess.com Premium, and tournament travel. Most of it flows through Wise, which handles her multi-currency life in one place.
What Mira Wants Out
At the end of every month, Mira needs answers:

• What came in across all currencies?
  • What went out, by category?
  • Which categories went over budget?
  • What should next month's budget look like?

She used to download CSV files from Wise and paste them into ChatGPT to analyze. But the file is outdated as soon as a new transaction comes in — and her finances move every day. Time to build her a new CustomGPT with access to the live data!

feedbackCorrect.text: A live-data GPT can pull up-to-date information, handle multi-currency realities, and surface uncertainty. The skill is connection plus restraint.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Five-year forecasts aren't the job Mira really needs. She wants to understand the month she just lived through. Live data, currency handling, and uncertainty surfacing are what matter for the monthly review.

options.label: Building detailed five-year financial forecasts
Surfacing uncertainty when transaction data is ambiguous
Handling multiple currencies without manual conversion
Pulling fresh data from Wise every time she asks

blocks.question: What would make Mira's Custom GPT genuinely useful for a monthly financial review?

blocks.text: Two Ways to Reach External Services
ChatGPT has two ways to reach external services. Both are useful, but they work differently:

• Plugins: reusable bundles that can contain skills and connect to apps (such as Booking.com, Canva, Spotify, etc.). Useful, but limited to what's in the library. You'll learn more about them in the next lesson.
  • Actions: custom integrations you configure inside a Custom GPT. More setup, more power. This lesson is exactly about them.
How Actions Work

Actions work through the API. An API (Application Programming Interface) is a way for one app to talk to another. For example, Wise is not in the ChatGPT App library, but it has an API that lets other tools — including ChatGPT — request transaction history, account balances, and conversion rates.
Building a Financial Assistant
Before connecting to any API, the Custom GPT still needs the foundation:

• Role
  • Instructions
  • Routing rules for ambiguous input.
And after the foundation is in place, the API connection gets added on top.
Connecting Mira's GPT to Wise

Most services with a public API publish their documentation online, usually at a developer page (search the service name + "API documentation" or "developer docs"). For Wise, that documentation lives on their developer site.
Inside the Custom GPT builder, open the Configure tab and scroll to Actions. The action needs a schema — a structured description of what the API can do.

You don't have to write it yourself! Click "Get help from ActionsGPT" — an OpenAI Custom GPT that turns API documentation into the OpenAPI schema your action needs. Share the link to Wise's API documentation and ask ActionsGPT to generate the schema. Then copy the result into the Schema field in the Custom GPT builder.

Then, set up authentication — this is how Wise verifies that the GPT has permission to access the account. Most services let you generate a personal API key in your account settings: open Wise, go to the developer section, generate the key, then paste it into ChatGPT.
First Live Question

Great job! With Wise connected, Mira asks her first live question, "What did I earn from teaching in June?" The GPT pulls from Wise and returns totals by student, currency, and week. The number matches her records. The connection works.

That first result is an important milestone: the connection works, and the GPT can answer from live data.

Next, Mira makes the setup more reliable by defining what should happen when the data is ambiguous or incomplete, or when the request falls outside the GPT's role.
Where Live Data Breaks

The failure modes for live-data GPTs are different from the ones in the previous lesson — they're about what comes back from the API, not what goes in from the user.

When the data is fuzzy, the GPT can confidently invent answers that look right. That's the new risk that live data introduces.
The Live-Data Failure Modes
Connecting to live data has some new ways in which GPT can potentially fail:

• Ambiguous source data: The API returns data that could mean multiple things.
  • Incomplete data: Recent transactions are still pending, but the GPT reports the totals as final.
  • Off-scope write request: The user asks the GPT to take an action it shouldn't.
Each one needs a rule. Let's go through them.
Failure Mode 1: Ambiguous Source Data

Mira asks, "What did I spend at Amazon this month?" The API returns 14 Amazon transactions. Two are clearly groceries — the memo says "Whole Foods via Amazon." The other twelve just say "Amazon $X.XX" — could be groceries, household items, work supplies, or gifts. Mira's GPT should surface the ambiguity.
Calibrated Confidence Gating
The rule that prevents fabrication is called Calibrated Confidence Gating. The GPT must hit a confidence threshold for each claim. Below the threshold, it stops and asks.
Where the Threshold Lives

The threshold is a rule you write into the Instructions field. The threshold you set is a behavioral instruction ChatGPT follows — you're telling it to judge its own certainty on each claim and stop when that judgment falls short. That's why the wording of the clause matters.

It's best to set the threshold in the instruction at these figures, so the AI performs best:
  • Higher than 85% when fabrication is expensive: medical info, legal claims, decisions tied to real money
  • 85% for most professional analysis: catches ambiguous cases, lets clean ones through
  • Lower than 85% when asking costs more than being slightly wrong — brainstorming, idea generation
blocks.title: 💡 The Threshold Is a Choice

blocks.prompt: Complete the routing rule in the Instructions that prevents the GPT from guessing under uncertainty.
blocks.template: If confidence in [data type] is below [threshold], [command] and ask me before proceeding

blocks.text: Failure Mode 2: Incomplete Data

Mira checks her spending at 11 p.m. on Sunday. Six of Saturday's card payments are still marked as pending and haven't settled yet. If the GPT reports only the settled transactions as the complete weekly total, the review is misleading. Spending and category totals may still change once those pending payments settle.

feedbackCorrect.text: Flagging the pending items gives Mira the choice. She might want the partial picture anyway for a quick check, or wait until everything settles. The GPT shouldn't decide silently — and refusing entirely is too strict for what's usually a small gap.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Including or dropping pending transactions silently leads to the same place — totals that don't match reality, with no warning. Refusing entirely overcorrects. The right move is transparency: name what's pending, let Mira decide.

options.label: Refuse to answer until every transaction settles
Silently include them — pending payments almost always go through
Flag the pending transactions and ask if Mira wants to proceed with partial totals
Quietly leave them out of the totals

blocks.question: The data Wise returns includes 6 card transactions still marked as pending. What should the gated GPT do?

blocks.text: Add a Check

You add one line to the same gating block where the confidence rule lives, so incomplete data trips the gate the way low-confidence claims do: "If the data includes pending or incomplete transactions, say so, show which totals they affect, and ask whether to include them."
Failure Mode 3: Off-Scope Write Requests
Mira types, "Create a new recipient in Wise for me." The GPT could call the Wise API to initiate the action — the connection is there; the permissions might allow it. But should it?
Access Policy
For every Action the GPT could take, there are four levels of scope:

• Read = can do without confirmation
  • Write with confirmation = proposes the action, waits for Mira's approval
  • Never without explicit config = possible to enable, but locked off by default
  • Out of scope entirely = refuses, regardless of how the request is phrased

For Mira's finance assistant, the settings can be: "read transactions freely, propose category labels for my review, create new recipients only after confirmation, never initiate payments, never transfer money."

feedbackCorrect.text: Creating a recipient changes data in Wise, so it belongs under "Write with confirmation". Mira can request it, but the GPT should wait for her explicit approval before making the change.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Creating a recipient isn't a read-only action — it changes the account. The GPT can prepare the action, but should only carry it out after Mira confirms.

blocks.instruction: For an action Mira might request, decide where it belongs in the access policy.

options.label: Read
Write with confirmation

blocks.question: "Create a new recipient in Wise for me."

blocks.text:
Two layers of protection against the new failure surface:
  • Calibrated Confidence Gating for ambiguous data. Ask before claiming.
  • Access policy for ambiguous actions. Refuse or confirm.
Together, they prevent the two most expensive failure classes of live-data integrations: confident wrong answers and unauthorized writes.
blocks.title: 💡 Gating Plus Policy

blocks.text: Mira's End-of-Month Review
With gating and policy in place, Mira runs her actual June review. The GPT pulls live data, surfaces ambiguities, rejects off-scope requests, and produces a clean health check.

blocks.exampleResponse: June Financial Review Income — 12 students across EUR, GBP, USD — Kids' monthly subscriptions: 8 students, paid on time — Adults' per-session payments: 4 students, 18 sessions total Spending by category — based on 84 transactions — Rent, groceries, subscriptions: clean categorization — 12 Amazon transactions flagged — could be groceries, household, or supplies. Confirm before final report? Data status — 2 card payments still pending — include now, or wait for them to settle? Multi-currency note — EUR and GBP totals shown in original amount and current conversion. Rates have shifted ~2% since transactions cleared — flagged in the breakdown. Off-scope request declined — "Pay my Chess.com subscription" — payments aren't in this GPT's scope. Handle directly in Wise. Ready to finalize the June summary and draft a July budget once the 12 Amazon items are categorized.
blocks.prompt: Mira asks her Custom GPT for a full monthly financial review. Complete the prompt.
blocks.template: Show [output] for June. Flag anything [flag condition] and surface across multiple currencies.

blocks.text: Great! June's review is done. The numbers match the records, the ambiguities are flagged for Mira to resolve, and she didn't have to download a single file!

• APIs let ChatGPT request live data from external services like Wise.
  • Plugins are pre-built, fast, but limited to the library. Actions are custom, configurable, and work with any API.
  • Calibrated Confidence Gating stops the GPT from claiming what it isn't sure about.
  • Access policy defines what the GPT can read, write, or refuse. Set the scope before connecting.
blocks.title: Key Takeaways

blocks.text: What's Next?

You've built a Custom GPT that connects to a single service and refuses to fabricate. The next lesson goes the other direction — using Plugins to connect ChatGPT to several services at once, building a personal assistant that handles your week across Calendar, Drive, Gmail, and more. Let's keep going!

blocks.text: Custom GPTs with Actions

In the previous lesson, you built Mira's coaching assistant. The Custom GPT holds 12 students' states and produces three different artifacts per student. Now it's time to add another layer.

Without live data, a Custom GPT can only work with what you've manually uploaded. To pull live data, like bank transactions, Custom GPTs require different settings. That's what this lesson covers.

Let's get started!
Mira's Other Sunday Problem

Lesson prep is solved. But every Sunday, Mira also sits down to check her finances — and that part still takes time.

End of June. It's time to check what came in, what went out, and plan for July.
Mira's money moves across multiple accounts and currencies. Her income looks like this:

• 8 kids on monthly subscriptions, paid by parents.
  • 4 adults paying per session, in USD, EUR, or GBP.
Her spending mixes personal and business: rent, groceries, Chess.com Premium, and tournament travel. Most of it flows through Wise, which handles her multi-currency life in one place.
What Mira Wants Out
At the end of every month, Mira needs answers:

• What came in across all currencies?
  • What went out, by category?
  • Which categories went over budget?
  • What should next month's budget look like?

She used to download CSV files from Wise and paste them into ChatGPT to analyze. But the file is outdated as soon as a new transaction comes in — and her finances move every day. Time to build her a new CustomGPT with access to the live data!

feedbackCorrect.text: A live-data GPT can pull up-to-date information, handle multi-currency realities, and surface uncertainty. The skill is connection plus restraint.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Five-year forecasts aren't the job Mira really needs. She wants to understand the month she just lived through. Live data, currency handling, and uncertainty surfacing are what matter for the monthly review.

options.label: Building detailed five-year financial forecasts
Surfacing uncertainty when transaction data is ambiguous
Handling multiple currencies without manual conversion
Pulling fresh data from Wise every time she asks

blocks.question: What would make Mira's Custom GPT genuinely useful for a monthly financial review?

blocks.text: Two Ways to Reach External Services
ChatGPT has two ways to reach external services. Both are useful, but they work differently:

• Plugins: reusable bundles that can contain skills and connect to apps (such as Booking.com, Canva, Spotify, etc.). Useful, but limited to what's in the library. You'll learn more about them in the next lesson.
  • Actions: custom integrations you configure inside a Custom GPT. More setup, more power. This lesson is exactly about them.
How Actions Work

Actions work through the API. An API (Application Programming Interface) is a way for one app to talk to another. For example, Wise is not in the ChatGPT App library, but it has an API that lets other tools — including ChatGPT — request transaction history, account balances, and conversion rates.
Building a Financial Assistant
Before connecting to any API, the Custom GPT still needs the foundation:

• Role
  • Instructions
  • Routing rules for ambiguous input.
And after the foundation is in place, the API connection gets added on top.
Connecting Mira's GPT to Wise

Most services with a public API publish their documentation online, usually at a developer page (search the service name + "API documentation" or "developer docs"). For Wise, that documentation lives on their developer site.
Inside the Custom GPT builder, open the Configure tab and scroll to Actions. The action needs a schema — a structured description of what the API can do.

You don't have to write it yourself! Click "Get help from ActionsGPT" — an OpenAI Custom GPT that turns API documentation into the OpenAPI schema your action needs. Share the link to Wise's API documentation and ask ActionsGPT to generate the schema. Then copy the result into the Schema field in the Custom GPT builder.

Then, set up authentication — this is how Wise verifies that the GPT has permission to access the account. Most services let you generate a personal API key in your account settings: open Wise, go to the developer section, generate the key, then paste it into ChatGPT.
First Live Question

Great job! With Wise connected, Mira asks her first live question, "What did I earn from teaching in June?" The GPT pulls from Wise and returns totals by student, currency, and week. The number matches her records. The connection works.

That first result is an important milestone: the connection works, and the GPT can answer from live data.

Next, Mira makes the setup more reliable by defining what should happen when the data is ambiguous or incomplete, or when the request falls outside the GPT's role.
Where Live Data Breaks

The failure modes for live-data GPTs are different from the ones in the previous lesson — they're about what comes back from the API, not what goes in from the user.

When the data is fuzzy, the GPT can confidently invent answers that look right. That's the new risk that live data introduces.
The Live-Data Failure Modes
Connecting to live data has some new ways in which GPT can potentially fail:

• Ambiguous source data: The API returns data that could mean multiple things.
  • Incomplete data: Recent transactions are still pending, but the GPT reports the totals as final.
  • Off-scope write request: The user asks the GPT to take an action it shouldn't.
Each one needs a rule. Let's go through them.
Failure Mode 1: Ambiguous Source Data

Mira asks, "What did I spend at Amazon this month?" The API returns 14 Amazon transactions. Two are clearly groceries — the memo says "Whole Foods via Amazon." The other twelve just say "Amazon $X.XX" — could be groceries, household items, work supplies, or gifts. Mira's GPT should surface the ambiguity.
Calibrated Confidence Gating
The rule that prevents fabrication is called Calibrated Confidence Gating. The GPT must hit a confidence threshold for each claim. Below the threshold, it stops and asks.
Where the Threshold Lives

The threshold is a rule you write into the Instructions field. The threshold you set is a behavioral instruction ChatGPT follows — you're telling it to judge its own certainty on each claim and stop when that judgment falls short. That's why the wording of the clause matters.

It's best to set the threshold in the instruction at these figures, so the AI performs best:
  • Higher than 85% when fabrication is expensive: medical info, legal claims, decisions tied to real money
  • 85% for most professional analysis: catches ambiguous cases, lets clean ones through
  • Lower than 85% when asking costs more than being slightly wrong — brainstorming, idea generation
blocks.title: 💡 The Threshold Is a Choice

blocks.prompt: Complete the routing rule in the Instructions that prevents the GPT from guessing under uncertainty.
blocks.template: If confidence in [data type] is below [threshold], [command] and ask me before proceeding

blocks.text: Failure Mode 2: Incomplete Data

Mira checks her spending at 11 p.m. on Sunday. Six of Saturday's card payments are still marked as pending and haven't settled yet. If the GPT reports only the settled transactions as the complete weekly total, the review is misleading. Spending and category totals may still change once those pending payments settle.

feedbackCorrect.text: Flagging the pending items gives Mira the choice. She might want the partial picture anyway for a quick check, or wait until everything settles. The GPT shouldn't decide silently — and refusing entirely is too strict for what's usually a small gap.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Including or dropping pending transactions silently leads to the same place — totals that don't match reality, with no warning. Refusing entirely overcorrects. The right move is transparency: name what's pending, let Mira decide.

options.label: Refuse to answer until every transaction settles
Silently include them — pending payments almost always go through
Flag the pending transactions and ask if Mira wants to proceed with partial totals
Quietly leave them out of the totals

blocks.question: The data Wise returns includes 6 card transactions still marked as pending. What should the gated GPT do?

blocks.text: Add a Check

You add one line to the same gating block where the confidence rule lives, so incomplete data trips the gate the way low-confidence claims do: "If the data includes pending or incomplete transactions, say so, show which totals they affect, and ask whether to include them."
Failure Mode 3: Off-Scope Write Requests
Mira types, "Create a new recipient in Wise for me." The GPT could call the Wise API to initiate the action — the connection is there; the permissions might allow it. But should it?
Access Policy
For every Action the GPT could take, there are four levels of scope:

• Read = can do without confirmation
  • Write with confirmation = proposes the action, waits for Mira's approval
  • Never without explicit config = possible to enable, but locked off by default
  • Out of scope entirely = refuses, regardless of how the request is phrased

For Mira's finance assistant, the settings can be: "read transactions freely, propose category labels for my review, create new recipients only after confirmation, never initiate payments, never transfer money."

feedbackCorrect.text: Creating a recipient changes data in Wise, so it belongs under "Write with confirmation". Mira can request it, but the GPT should wait for her explicit approval before making the change.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Creating a recipient isn't a read-only action — it changes the account. The GPT can prepare the action, but should only carry it out after Mira confirms.

blocks.instruction: For an action Mira might request, decide where it belongs in the access policy.

options.label: Read
Write with confirmation

blocks.question: "Create a new recipient in Wise for me."

blocks.text:
Two layers of protection against the new failure surface:
  • Calibrated Confidence Gating for ambiguous data. Ask before claiming.
  • Access policy for ambiguous actions. Refuse or confirm.
Together, they prevent the two most expensive failure classes of live-data integrations: confident wrong answers and unauthorized writes.
blocks.title: 💡 Gating Plus Policy

blocks.text: Mira's End-of-Month Review
With gating and policy in place, Mira runs her actual June review. The GPT pulls live data, surfaces ambiguities, rejects off-scope requests, and produces a clean health check.

blocks.exampleResponse: June Financial Review Income — 12 students across EUR, GBP, USD — Kids' monthly subscriptions: 8 students, paid on time — Adults' per-session payments: 4 students, 18 sessions total Spending by category — based on 84 transactions — Rent, groceries, subscriptions: clean categorization — 12 Amazon transactions flagged — could be groceries, household, or supplies. Confirm before final report? Data status — 2 card payments still pending — include now, or wait for them to settle? Multi-currency note — EUR and GBP totals shown in original amount and current conversion. Rates have shifted ~2% since transactions cleared — flagged in the breakdown. Off-scope request declined — "Pay my Chess.com subscription" — payments aren't in this GPT's scope. Handle directly in Wise. Ready to finalize the June summary and draft a July budget once the 12 Amazon items are categorized.
blocks.prompt: Mira asks her Custom GPT for a full monthly financial review. Complete the prompt.
blocks.template: Show [output] for June. Flag anything [flag condition] and surface across multiple currencies.

blocks.text: Great! June's review is done. The numbers match the records, the ambiguities are flagged for Mira to resolve, and she didn't have to download a single file!

• APIs let ChatGPT request live data from external services like Wise.
  • Plugins are pre-built, fast, but limited to the library. Actions are custom, configurable, and work with any API.
  • Calibrated Confidence Gating stops the GPT from claiming what it isn't sure about.
  • Access policy defines what the GPT can read, write, or refuse. Set the scope before connecting.
blocks.title: Key Takeaways

blocks.text: What's Next?

You've built a Custom GPT that connects to a single service and refuses to fabricate. The next lesson goes the other direction — using Plugins to connect ChatGPT to several services at once, building a personal assistant that handles your week across Calendar, Drive, Gmail, and more. Let's keep going!

lessons.title: Custom GPTs: Connecting to External Systems

blocks.text: The Personal Assistant That Runs Your Week

Your week lives in pieces: appointments in one app, emails in another, and a to-do list partly in your head.

Every Monday, you stitch everything together by hand. But one conversation can pull it all into a single view instead! By the end of this lesson, you'll connect several Plugins at once and build an assistant that does exactly that.

Let's get started!
Scenario: Handling Household Logistics

Naomi works part-time in marketing and has two kids, aged 7 and 11. She runs the household logistics.

The load is real but invisible, scattered across her calendar, her inbox, some shared docs, and a Notion tracker she set up last year.
The Monday Problem

Every Monday, she pieces the week together by hand. Check the calendar. Scroll through the inbox for school emails. Open the meal-plan doc. Cross-check both kids' activities against her own work shifts.

20-30 minutes of tab-switching before she even knows what the week needs from her.
Where It All Lives
Naomi's week is spread across four tools:

• Calendar: appointments, kids' activities, her work shifts
  • Gmail: school emails, activity sign-ups, confirmations
  • Drive: permission slips, forms, the family budget
  • Notion: the meal plan, chores, the running to-do list
Each holds one piece, and none of them talks to each other.

feedbackCorrect.text: The problem is too much information across too many places, with no single view. Naomi spends her time gathering and cross-checking rather than deciding.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Naomi has plenty of information. The issue is that it lives in four disconnected tools, so she does the gathering and cross-referencing by hand every single week.

options.label: The information is scattered across separate tools
Nothing pulls everything together automatically
She has to manually cross-check each source against the others
She doesn't have enough information to plan the week

blocks.question: What makes Naomi's Monday prep so slow?

blocks.text: Connecting More Than One

ChatGPT can organize connected workflows through plugins. A plugin can package skills, app integrations, and reusable setup for a particular job. The apps inside it connect ChatGPT to external services such as your calendar, inbox, or document storage. You've probably connected an app before. The new move here is to use multiple connected apps in a single prompt. ChatGPT can retrieve relevant information from each source and combine it into one response.
Apps And Their Capabilities

Apps inside plugins can have different capabilities. Some can search and reference connected information, some can show interactive experiences in the chat, and some can take actions. For Naomi's assistant, the key capabilities are search and reference: ChatGPT pulls relevant information from her connected sources and combines it into a single brief.
Finding the Plugins
It's time for Naomi to connect her plugins. Connecting starts in the Plugins panel. Open it from the sidebar, and you'll see a directory of available services grouped into categories.

Naomi searches for each tool she needs by name: Google Calendar, Gmail, Drive, and Notion. Each one shows a short description, the app it connects to, the skills that become available, and other important information.
Connecting Each One

For each plugin, Naomi clicks Install Plugin and signs in to that service. The plugin asks what it's allowed to access — for Calendar, that's her events; for Gmail, her messages — and she approves. Once connected, the plugin stays available across the conversation. She repeats this for all four, and the assistant can now reach every source at once.
Before connecting personal accounts, review the access each app requests and your ChatGPT data settings. Connect only the sources you are comfortable using in the workflow.
blocks.title: 💡 Before You Connect

blocks.text: The First Brief

With everything connected, Naomi asks for what she wants: a single view of the week ahead, built from all four sources at once.

Let's see what she types.

blocks.exampleResponse: Your Week — Monday, July 6 Appointments & Activities — Tue: Dentist (Lena, 3 p.m.), Piano (Leo, 4 p.m.) — Wed: Your work deadline, Soccer practice (Leo, 5 p.m.) From your inbox — School permission slip — due Wednesday — Swim class sign-up — closes Friday — Two unread school newsletters Meal plan — Low on: milk, eggs, pasta — Thursday dinner not yet planned
blocks.prompt: Complete the prompt that pulls Naomi's whole week into one view.
blocks.template: [Command] my week ahead. Pull [calendar data] from Calendar, [inbox data] from Gmail, and the meal plan from Notion.

blocks.text: It Worked — But Look Closer

Nicely done! In one conversation, ChatGPT pulled from four sources to build a single view. No tab-switching or manual cross-checking required. But look at the brief again. Everything is listed flat — the permission slip due Wednesday sits in the same plain list as "low on milk." Nothing tells Naomi what needs her first.

feedbackCorrect.text: The synthesis worked, but a flat list hides urgency. A permission slip due tomorrow deserves more attention than a grocery note, and the brief treats them the same.

feedbackIncorrect.text: The plugins connected successfully, and the brief has plenty of detail. The real issue is that everything sits at the same level, so Naomi still has to scan and prioritize herself.

options.label: Time-critical items are buried next to low-priority ones
The brief contains too few items to be useful
The plugins didn't connect to each other properly

blocks.question: The brief pulled everything correctly, but listed it flat. What's the problem with that?

blocks.text: Teaching ChatGPT to Prioritize

A useful assistant ranks tasks by urgency.

Naomi adds one instruction: sort everything by urgency, surface what needs her today or this week first, and push the informational items to the bottom.

One line changes the brief into a plan with clear priorities.

blocks.exampleResponse: This Week — Ranked Needs attention first — Dentist appointment — Lena, Tuesday, 3 p.m. — Piano — Leo, Tuesday, 4 p.m. — Permission slip — due Wednesday — Work deadline — Wednesday Later this week — Soccer practice — Leo, Wednesday, 5 p.m. — Swim class sign-up — closes Friday — Thursday dinner not yet planned When you get a chance — Restock milk, eggs, pasta — Two unread school newsletters
blocks.prompt: Complete the instruction that ranks the brief by what matters most.
blocks.template: Rank everything by [ranking criterion]. Surface [top tier] first, then everything else. Move informational notes to the end.

blocks.text: A Brief That Is Useful

Great! Now, Naomi can see what needs attention first without having to scan the whole brief herself. The nearest appointments and deadlines sit at the top, while lower-priority notes move out of the way.

Bringing information together is only half the job.
  • Retrieval: Find the relevant information across the connected plugins.
  • Verification: Check important dates and details against the original sources.
  • Ranking: Sort the verified items by urgency and importance.
blocks.title: 💡 Synthesis Needs Structure

blocks.text: What Stays Connected

Naomi's assistant works. Now she can make the setup more deliberate. Her information may be spread across four tools, but not every source needs to be part of every weekly brief. Some sources are useful all the time. Others are sensitive or only needed for specific tasks.
Recurring vs. Task-Scoped Sources
Naomi splits her sources into two groups:

• Recurring sources: tools she uses for every weekly brief and is comfortable keeping available for that workflow.
  • Task-scoped sources: sensitive or occasional sources she brings in only when a specific task requires them.
Calendar, Gmail, and Notion belong in Naomi's recurring workflow. The Drive folder with medical and financial documents stays task-scoped.
Keep sensitive or occasional sources out of the recurring workflow, and use them only when the task requires them.
blocks.title: Connect Only What You Need

feedbackCorrect.text: Passports and travel documents are sensitive and only required occasionally. Connect the folder when you're actually planning a trip, then leave it out of the everyday assistant.

feedbackIncorrect.text: This is task-scoped. High-sensitivity documents used only now and then shouldn't sit in a permanently connected assistant — pull them in for the specific task, then disconnect.

blocks.instruction: Decide whether this source belongs in the standing assistant or should stay task-scoped.

options.label: Always connected
Task-scoped

blocks.question: A folder of scanned passports and travel documents, opened only when booking trips

blocks.text: From Information to Action

Naomi's assistant tells her the permission slip is due on Wednesday. The natural next thought: can it reply to the school email for me? That's a different capability. This assistant informs — it tells her what the week needs. Making it act — reply, book, submit — is the next layer. You'll learn about it in the next lesson.

blocks.prompt: Arrange the steps to build a personal assistant that pulls together recurring tasks.
blocks.title: Building the Assistant

blocks.text: Beyond Naomi's Monday
The pattern transfers to any recurring task spread across tools:

• A Monday work brief: Calendar + Drive + Slack
  • A freelance week-ahead: Calendar + Gmail + an invoicing app
  • A study-week plan: Calendar + Drive + Notion
Same structure every time: connect the sources, synthesize into one view, rank by what you need first.
The Result
Naomi's Monday prep used to take half an hour of opening tabs and cross-checking. Now it's one short conversation — the week pulled together, ranked, and ready before she starts her morning coffee.

• Connecting several plugins at once lets ChatGPT draw on all of them in a single conversation.
  • Reference plugins gather data; interactive ones work in chat.
  • A multi-source brief needs prioritization, such as an urgency rank.
  • Keep daily-driver plugins connected and sensitive plugins task-scoped.
  • Synthesis tells you what needs to be done. Making the assistant act on it is the next step.
blocks.title: Key Takeaways

blocks.text: What's Next?

Naomi's assistant tells her what the week needs. The next lesson goes one step further — connecting plugins in sequence, so ChatGPT acts across them: read an email, pull out the task, create it on a board, all in one flow. Let's keep going!

blocks.text: The Personal Assistant That Runs Your Week

Your week lives in pieces: appointments in one app, emails in another, and a to-do list partly in your head.

Every Monday, you stitch everything together by hand. But one conversation can pull it all into a single view instead! By the end of this lesson, you'll connect several Plugins at once and build an assistant that does exactly that.

Let's get started!
Scenario: Handling Household Logistics

Naomi works part-time in marketing and has two kids, aged 7 and 11. She runs the household logistics.

The load is real but invisible, scattered across her calendar, her inbox, some shared docs, and a Notion tracker she set up last year.
The Monday Problem

Every Monday, she pieces the week together by hand. Check the calendar. Scroll through the inbox for school emails. Open the meal-plan doc. Cross-check both kids' activities against her own work shifts.

20-30 minutes of tab-switching before she even knows what the week needs from her.
Where It All Lives
Naomi's week is spread across four tools:

• Calendar: appointments, kids' activities, her work shifts
  • Gmail: school emails, activity sign-ups, confirmations
  • Drive: permission slips, forms, the family budget
  • Notion: the meal plan, chores, the running to-do list
Each holds one piece, and none of them talks to each other.

feedbackCorrect.text: The problem is too much information across too many places, with no single view. Naomi spends her time gathering and cross-checking rather than deciding.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Naomi has plenty of information. The issue is that it lives in four disconnected tools, so she does the gathering and cross-referencing by hand every single week.

options.label: The information is scattered across separate tools
Nothing pulls everything together automatically
She has to manually cross-check each source against the others
She doesn't have enough information to plan the week

blocks.question: What makes Naomi's Monday prep so slow?

blocks.text: Connecting More Than One

ChatGPT can organize connected workflows through plugins. A plugin can package skills, app integrations, and reusable setup for a particular job. The apps inside it connect ChatGPT to external services such as your calendar, inbox, or document storage. You've probably connected an app before. The new move here is to use multiple connected apps in a single prompt. ChatGPT can retrieve relevant information from each source and combine it into one response.
Apps And Their Capabilities

Apps inside plugins can have different capabilities. Some can search and reference connected information, some can show interactive experiences in the chat, and some can take actions. For Naomi's assistant, the key capabilities are search and reference: ChatGPT pulls relevant information from her connected sources and combines it into a single brief.
Finding the Plugins
It's time for Naomi to connect her plugins. Connecting starts in the Plugins panel. Open it from the sidebar, and you'll see a directory of available services grouped into categories.

Naomi searches for each tool she needs by name: Google Calendar, Gmail, Drive, and Notion. Each one shows a short description, the app it connects to, the skills that become available, and other important information.
Connecting Each One

For each plugin, Naomi clicks Install Plugin and signs in to that service. The plugin asks what it's allowed to access — for Calendar, that's her events; for Gmail, her messages — and she approves. Once connected, the plugin stays available across the conversation. She repeats this for all four, and the assistant can now reach every source at once.
Before connecting personal accounts, review the access each app requests and your ChatGPT data settings. Connect only the sources you are comfortable using in the workflow.
blocks.title: 💡 Before You Connect

blocks.text: The First Brief

With everything connected, Naomi asks for what she wants: a single view of the week ahead, built from all four sources at once.

Let's see what she types.

blocks.exampleResponse: Your Week — Monday, July 6 Appointments & Activities — Tue: Dentist (Lena, 3 p.m.), Piano (Leo, 4 p.m.) — Wed: Your work deadline, Soccer practice (Leo, 5 p.m.) From your inbox — School permission slip — due Wednesday — Swim class sign-up — closes Friday — Two unread school newsletters Meal plan — Low on: milk, eggs, pasta — Thursday dinner not yet planned
blocks.prompt: Complete the prompt that pulls Naomi's whole week into one view.
blocks.template: [Command] my week ahead. Pull [calendar data] from Calendar, [inbox data] from Gmail, and the meal plan from Notion.

blocks.text: It Worked — But Look Closer

Nicely done! In one conversation, ChatGPT pulled from four sources to build a single view. No tab-switching or manual cross-checking required. But look at the brief again. Everything is listed flat — the permission slip due Wednesday sits in the same plain list as "low on milk." Nothing tells Naomi what needs her first.

feedbackCorrect.text: The synthesis worked, but a flat list hides urgency. A permission slip due tomorrow deserves more attention than a grocery note, and the brief treats them the same.

feedbackIncorrect.text: The plugins connected successfully, and the brief has plenty of detail. The real issue is that everything sits at the same level, so Naomi still has to scan and prioritize herself.

options.label: Time-critical items are buried next to low-priority ones
The brief contains too few items to be useful
The plugins didn't connect to each other properly

blocks.question: The brief pulled everything correctly, but listed it flat. What's the problem with that?

blocks.text: Teaching ChatGPT to Prioritize

A useful assistant ranks tasks by urgency.

Naomi adds one instruction: sort everything by urgency, surface what needs her today or this week first, and push the informational items to the bottom.

One line changes the brief into a plan with clear priorities.

blocks.exampleResponse: This Week — Ranked Needs attention first — Dentist appointment — Lena, Tuesday, 3 p.m. — Piano — Leo, Tuesday, 4 p.m. — Permission slip — due Wednesday — Work deadline — Wednesday Later this week — Soccer practice — Leo, Wednesday, 5 p.m. — Swim class sign-up — closes Friday — Thursday dinner not yet planned When you get a chance — Restock milk, eggs, pasta — Two unread school newsletters
blocks.prompt: Complete the instruction that ranks the brief by what matters most.
blocks.template: Rank everything by [ranking criterion]. Surface [top tier] first, then everything else. Move informational notes to the end.

blocks.text: A Brief That Is Useful

Great! Now, Naomi can see what needs attention first without having to scan the whole brief herself. The nearest appointments and deadlines sit at the top, while lower-priority notes move out of the way.

Bringing information together is only half the job.
  • Retrieval: Find the relevant information across the connected plugins.
  • Verification: Check important dates and details against the original sources.
  • Ranking: Sort the verified items by urgency and importance.
blocks.title: 💡 Synthesis Needs Structure

blocks.text: What Stays Connected

Naomi's assistant works. Now she can make the setup more deliberate. Her information may be spread across four tools, but not every source needs to be part of every weekly brief. Some sources are useful all the time. Others are sensitive or only needed for specific tasks.
Recurring vs. Task-Scoped Sources
Naomi splits her sources into two groups:

• Recurring sources: tools she uses for every weekly brief and is comfortable keeping available for that workflow.
  • Task-scoped sources: sensitive or occasional sources she brings in only when a specific task requires them.
Calendar, Gmail, and Notion belong in Naomi's recurring workflow. The Drive folder with medical and financial documents stays task-scoped.
Keep sensitive or occasional sources out of the recurring workflow, and use them only when the task requires them.
blocks.title: Connect Only What You Need

feedbackCorrect.text: Passports and travel documents are sensitive and only required occasionally. Connect the folder when you're actually planning a trip, then leave it out of the everyday assistant.

feedbackIncorrect.text: This is task-scoped. High-sensitivity documents used only now and then shouldn't sit in a permanently connected assistant — pull them in for the specific task, then disconnect.

Task-scoped

blocks.text: What's Next?

Naomi's assistant tells her what the week needs. The next lesson goes one step further — connecting plugins in sequence, so ChatGPT acts across them: read an email, pull out the task, create it on a board, all in one flow. Let's keep going!
When Plugins Hand Off to Each Other

Last lesson, your assistant told you what the week needed. In this one, it does the work for you, such as reading from one app and acting in another, all in one flow. That's a new kind of power. By the end, you'll build a workflow that reads your inbox and creates the tasks — and know exactly where it can break.
Scenario: Small Business Expansion

Imagine this: you run a small café that's doing well. Well enough that you're opening a second location in 6 weeks. You're coordinating the whole launch while still running the original.

Almost all of the launch information lives in your Outlook inbox:

• Vendor quotes
  • Hiring threads
  • Contractor updates.
And every email turns into an Asana task for someone on your team.
Turning emails into tasks is tedious:

• You re-read each email to pull out the actual task.
  • You manually copy and paste the details into Asana.
  • You have to decide which task belongs to whom.

feedbackCorrect.text: The workflow needs to retrieve the email, map its details to the right Asana fields, and create the task. That removes the manual transfer between the two apps.

feedbackIncorrect.text: A summary may make the email faster to read, but you would still have to open Asana and enter the task yourself. The workflow needs to carry the information into Asana for you.

options.label: Match Tom to the correct Asana assignee
Read the email and extract the task details
Create the task in Asana
Summarize the email for you to enter manually

blocks.question: An email says, "Tom, order the espresso machine by Friday for the new location." Which steps must the workflow complete to turn it into a ready-to-use Asana task without manual re-entry?

blocks.text: A Tool That Acts

That's exactly what a connected workflow can do: read the email, pull out the task, and put it on the board in the same flow, asking for approval when required. But it's a different kind of help than you've seen so far.
From Informing to Acting

In the previous lesson, Naomi's assistant gathered information and told her what the week needed. Useful for her needs — but she still did the doing. Your workflow goes one step further. It reads the email and creates the task itself. That shift, from informing to acting, is what this lesson is about.
Connecting the Two Plugins
You already know how to connect plugins from the previous lesson. You need to connect Outlook and Asana — one to read from and one to write to. The new part is making one feed the other.
What a Handoff Is
A handoff passes information from one connected app into the fields another app needs. The workflow has four steps:

1. You: Ask ChatGPT to process a specific email.
  2. Outlook: Returns the matching email.
  3. ChatGPT: Extracts the task and maps it to structured fields.
  4. Asana: Creates the task, after approval, if one is required.
The workflow runs when you invoke it.

The heart of a handoff is turning loose text into structured fields. An email is loose text. An Asana task has slots: a name, a due date, an assignee, and a project. So when an email says, "Elena, can you have the menu ready before we open Saturday?" the GPT has to map that into:

• Task = finalize menu
  • Due = Friday
  • Assignee = Elena

blocks.exampleResponse: Task created in Asana — Task: Order the espresso machine for the new location — Due: Friday, Nov 22 — Assignee: Tom (build & equipment) — Project: Second Location Launch Pulled from the email: "Tom, can you get the espresso machine ordered by the end of the week so it's installed in time?"
blocks.prompt: In a chat with Outlook and Asana connected, you add an email to the workflow. Complete the instruction that turns it into a task.
blocks.template: Read the email in my Outlook from this Tuesday about the espresso machine. Create [output] with a clear [field], the correct due date, and the right assignee.

blocks.text: When It Works and When It Doesn't

Nicely done! One clear email, one clean task. The handoff did exactly what you wanted — read, extract, create, and assign.

But your real inbox isn't one clean email at a time. The next message can break the workflow.
Failure 1: One Task, Many Jobs

You get a planning email: "By the soft launch on the 14th, Elena needs to lock the menu, Tom needs to get the espresso machine installed, and Sam needs to post the hiring ad." Three asks and three different owners. But the workflow creates one task with all of it crammed inside. Both ends worked — it read the email and made a task — but the handoff flattened three jobs into one.
Where Handoffs Break

With a single plugin, problems mostly come from the input — something missing or unclear in what you typed. Multi-app workflows add another failure point: the mapping between steps. The email reads fine. The task gets created fine. The gap — the handoff point — is the new thing to watch.
Let's practice and see how to fix the email issue.

blocks.exampleResponse: 3 tasks created — Lock the menu → Elena · due Nov 14 — Install the espresso machine → Tom · due Nov 14 — Post the hiring ad → Sam · due Nov 14 Each ask became its own task, with its owner. The shared deadline applied to all three because the email tied them to the same launch date.
blocks.prompt: Complete the rule that tells the workflow to break a multi-part email into separate tasks.
blocks.template: When an email contains [condition], create [output], each with its own [reference person].

blocks.text: Failure 2: Name Confusion

Another email: "Jordan should own the launch-day social posts." Simple enough — except your team has two Jordans, and the workflow has to pick one. A name in an email doesn't always map cleanly to a person on the board. That's the assignee-mapping problem.
Fixing the Issue

The fix is the same instinct from earlier lessons: when something is ambiguous, confirm before acting. Now it applies to the handoff.

The rule: when a name in an email matches more than one person on the board, the workflow pauses and asks you which one to assign before continuing.
Failure 3: The Wrong Date

One more email: "Can you send the final menu to the printer by the 7th? The new location opens on the 12th." The workflow creates the right task — send the final menu to the printer — but sets the due date to the 12th. Both dates are real. But only one is the deadline for this task.
Fixing the Date
The fix is to tell the workflow which date is relevant. The due date should be the date tied to the action being created.
Here, “send the final menu to the printer” is due on the 7th. The 12th is the opening date, so it belongs in the task context rather than the due-date field.

Set the clear rule: Match each date to the action or event it describes. Don't choose a date just because it appears first, last, or closest to the task in the email. Identify what each date refers to, then place it in the right field.
Recovering Without Restarting

When a handoff breaks, you don't redo the whole run. The other tasks are fine — only the broken handoff needs fixing.

Wrong Jordan assigned? Reassign that one task. Wrong date pulled? Correct that one field. The rest of the board stands. Repairing the handoff beats rebuilding from scratch.

feedbackCorrect.text: Only one handoff broke, so only one task needs fixing. Reassign it and move on. The other four were correct — redoing them wastes the work the workflow already got right.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Deleting everything or starting over throws away four correct tasks to fix one. A handoff failure is local: repair the single broken handoff, not the whole run.

options.label: Start a new conversation to rebuild the workflow
Reassign that one task and leave the other four
Delete all five tasks and re-run the email

blocks.question: The workflow created five tasks correctly, but assigned one to the wrong Jordan. What's the right fix?

blocks.text: The Result

Great job! Your launch board no longer requires manual retyping from the inbox. When you ask ChatGPT to process the relevant emails, it turns them into assigned, dated tasks and pauses when something needs clarification or approval.
Beyond Your Café
The email-to-task shape is everywhere:

• Support emails → tickets in a tracker
  • Lead emails → records in a CRM
  • Meeting recaps → action items on a board
Same structure each time: read the source, extract the pieces, confirm the handoff, create the output.

• A handoff maps information between apps: It turns unstructured input into the structured fields the next app needs.
  • Multi-app workflows add a new failure point: Even when both apps work correctly, the handoff can map the wrong task, assignee, or date.
  • Split one input when it contains multiple asks: Create one output per ask so separate jobs don't get crammed into a single task.
  • Fix the broken result, not the whole workflow: When a handoff fails, repair the affected task or field and keep the rest intact.

blocks.text: What's Next?

Your workflow is running! Next, you'll capture the method behind recurring work. You'll build a reusable Skill that keeps the same rules, checks, and output structure ready for the next time a task comes back.

Let's keep going!
