And every email turns into an Asana task for someone on your team.
Turning emails into tasks is tedious:

• You re-read each email to pull out the actual task.
  • You manually copy and paste the details into Asana.
  • You have to decide which task belongs to whom.

feedbackCorrect.text: The workflow needs to retrieve the email, map its details to the right Asana fields, and create the task. That removes the manual transfer between the two apps.

feedbackIncorrect.text: A summary may make the email faster to read, but you would still have to open Asana and enter the task yourself. The workflow needs to carry the information into Asana for you.

options.label: Match Tom to the correct Asana assignee
Read the email and extract the task details
Create the task in Asana
Summarize the email for you to enter manually

blocks.question: An email says, "Tom, order the espresso machine by Friday for the new location." Which steps must the workflow complete to turn it into a ready-to-use Asana task without manual re-entry?

blocks.text: A Tool That Acts

That's exactly what a connected workflow can do: read the email, pull out the task, and put it on the board in the same flow, asking for approval when required. But it's a different kind of help than you've seen so far.
From Informing to Acting

In the previous lesson, Naomi's assistant gathered information and told her what the week needed. Useful for her needs — but she still did the doing. Your workflow goes one step further. It reads the email and creates the task itself. That shift, from informing to acting, is what this lesson is about.
Connecting the Two Plugins
You already know how to connect plugins from the previous lesson. You need to connect Outlook and Asana — one to read from and one to write to. The new part is making one feed the other.
What a Handoff Is
A handoff passes information from one connected app into the fields another app needs. The workflow has four steps:

1. You: Ask ChatGPT to process a specific email.
  2. Outlook: Returns the matching email.
  3. ChatGPT: Extracts the task and maps it to structured fields.
  4. Asana: Creates the task, after approval, if one is required.
The workflow runs when you invoke it.

The heart of a handoff is turning loose text into structured fields. An email is loose text. An Asana task has slots: a name, a due date, an assignee, and a project. So when an email says, "Elena, can you have the menu ready before we open Saturday?" the GPT has to map that into:

• Task = finalize menu
  • Due = Friday
  • Assignee = Elena

blocks.exampleResponse: Task created in Asana — Task: Order the espresso machine for the new location — Due: Friday, Nov 22 — Assignee: Tom (build & equipment) — Project: Second Location Launch Pulled from the email: "Tom, can you get the espresso machine ordered by the end of the week so it's installed in time?"
blocks.prompt: In a chat with Outlook and Asana connected, you add an email to the workflow. Complete the instruction that turns it into a task.
blocks.template: Read the email in my Outlook from this Tuesday about the espresso machine. Create [output] with a clear [field], the correct due date, and the right assignee.

blocks.text: When It Works and When It Doesn't

Nicely done! One clear email, one clean task. The handoff did exactly what you wanted — read, extract, create, and assign.

But your real inbox isn't one clean email at a time. The next message can break the workflow.
Failure 1: One Task, Many Jobs

You get a planning email: "By the soft launch on the 14th, Elena needs to lock the menu, Tom needs to get the espresso machine installed, and Sam needs to post the hiring ad." Three asks and three different owners. But the workflow creates one task with all of it crammed inside. Both ends worked — it read the email and made a task — but the handoff flattened three jobs into one.
Where Handoffs Break

With a single plugin, problems mostly come from the input — something missing or unclear in what you typed. Multi-app workflows add another failure point: the mapping between steps. The email reads fine. The task gets created fine. The gap — the handoff point — is the new thing to watch.
Let's practice and see how to fix the email issue.

blocks.exampleResponse: 3 tasks created — Lock the menu → Elena · due Nov 14 — Install the espresso machine → Tom · due Nov 14 — Post the hiring ad → Sam · due Nov 14 Each ask became its own task, with its owner. The shared deadline applied to all three because the email tied them to the same launch date.
blocks.prompt: Complete the rule that tells the workflow to break a multi-part email into separate tasks.
blocks.template: When an email contains [condition], create [output], each with its own [reference person].

blocks.text: Failure 2: Name Confusion

Another email: "Jordan should own the launch-day social posts." Simple enough — except your team has two Jordans, and the workflow has to pick one. A name in an email doesn't always map cleanly to a person on the board. That's the assignee-mapping problem.
Fixing the Issue

The fix is the same instinct from earlier lessons: when something is ambiguous, confirm before acting. Now it applies to the handoff.

The rule: when a name in an email matches more than one person on the board, the workflow pauses and asks you which one to assign before continuing.
Failure 3: The Wrong Date

One more email: "Can you send the final menu to the printer by the 7th? The new location opens on the 12th." The workflow creates the right task — send the final menu to the printer — but sets the due date to the 12th. Both dates are real. But only one is the deadline for this task.
Fixing the Date
The fix is to tell the workflow which date is relevant. The due date should be the date tied to the action being created.
Here, “send the final menu to the printer” is due on the 7th. The 12th is the opening date, so it belongs in the task context rather than the due-date field.

Set the clear rule: Match each date to the action or event it describes. Don't choose a date just because it appears first, last, or closest to the task in the email. Identify what each date refers to, then place it in the right field.
Recovering Without Restarting

When a handoff breaks, you don't redo the whole run. The other tasks are fine — only the broken handoff needs fixing.

Wrong Jordan assigned? Reassign that one task. Wrong date pulled? Correct that one field. The rest of the board stands. Repairing the handoff beats rebuilding from scratch.

feedbackCorrect.text: Only one handoff broke, so only one task needs fixing. Reassign it and move on. The other four were correct — redoing them wastes the work the workflow already got right.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Deleting everything or starting over throws away four correct tasks to fix one. A handoff failure is local: repair the single broken handoff, not the whole run.

options.label: Start a new conversation to rebuild the workflow
Reassign that one task and leave the other four
Delete all five tasks and re-run the email

blocks.question: The workflow created five tasks correctly, but assigned one to the wrong Jordan. What's the right fix?

blocks.text: The Result

Great job! Your launch board no longer requires manual retyping from the inbox. When you ask ChatGPT to process the relevant emails, it turns them into assigned, dated tasks and pauses when something needs clarification or approval.
Beyond Your Café
The email-to-task shape is everywhere:

• Support emails → tickets in a tracker
  • Lead emails → records in a CRM
  • Meeting recaps → action items on a board
Same structure each time: read the source, extract the pieces, confirm the handoff, create the output.

• A handoff maps information between apps: It turns unstructured input into the structured fields the next app needs.
  • Multi-app workflows add a new failure point: Even when both apps work correctly, the handoff can map the wrong task, assignee, or date.
  • Split one input when it contains multiple asks: Create one output per ask so separate jobs don't get crammed into a single task.
  • Fix the broken result, not the whole workflow: When a handoff fails, repair the affected task or field and keep the rest intact.
blocks.title: Key Takeaways

blocks.text: What's Next?

Your workflow is running! Next, you'll capture the method behind recurring work. You'll build a reusable Skill that keeps the same rules, checks, and output structure ready for the next time a task comes back.

Let's keep going!
Build a Skill That Makes Your Work Count

Imagine a promotion review is approaching. You know you've done strong work — but the proof is scattered across reports, experiment notes, dashboards, and stakeholder feedback. In this lesson, you'll build a personal ChatGPT Skill that provides real proof of work and turns your strongest achievements into a promotion-ready evidence table. Let's get started!
The Promotion Case Hidden in Your Files
You're a marketing analyst preparing for promotion to a senior position. You have your key results scattered over four important files:

• A campaign performance report
  • An experiment summary
  • Stakeholder feedback
  • The company's promotion framework
The hard part is proving exactly what you contributed.
The Real Task Isn't Better Writing
A useful promotion case applies the same judgment to every achievement:

• Separate personal contribution from team results.
  • Preserve only metrics supported by the evidence.
  • Map each achievement to the relevant competency.
  • Rate the evidence and flag anything that remains unproven.
You could paste these rules into every new chat, or teach ChatGPT the process once.
The Missing Layer

In the previous lessons, you changed what ChatGPT could reach and do: you built a Custom GPT, connected an API, brought in external apps, and passed information between them. This task has a different problem. The tools are already there. What you need to preserve is the method: the same evidence rules, checks, and output structure every time a new promotion review comes around. That's where a Skill comes in.
Meet Skills
A Skill is a reusable workflow that tells ChatGPT how to handle a specific task consistently. It can keep:

• The steps ChatGPT should follow
  • The required output format
  • Examples, templates, and reference materials
  • Rules about what to include or avoid

Once installed, ChatGPT can automatically use a relevant Skill from the triggers. You can also choose it yourself with an "@" mention in ChatGPT Work, or explicitly mention the Skill you want to use in the prompt.
Why a Skill, Not Another Custom GPT?

A Custom GPT gives you a dedicated assistant for a broader role or use case. A Skill is different: it preserves one reusable method that ChatGPT can apply whenever that task comes up. In your case, every promotion review brings new evidence. But the way you evaluate that evidence stays the same. You need the same review method applied to each fresh evidence pack.

feedbackCorrect.text: A Skill fits because it's a focused method you want ChatGPT to apply whenever the same type of task comes up. It preserves the steps and standards without requiring a separate assistant.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Not quite. Custom GPT would create a dedicated assistant with its own broader setup. Here, you only need ChatGPT to reuse a specific review method, which is what a Skill is designed for.

blocks.text: A Skill or a Plugin?

You also used Plugins — installable packages that can include Skills, connected apps, or both — for workflows that imply connections to external services. For the promotion task, you don't need a new service. You need ChatGPT to apply the same evidence rules every time, so you'll create a Skill.

feedbackCorrect.text: A Plugin can package a workflow together with the apps or other capabilities it needs. A Skill is enough when the reusable method itself is the main thing you want to preserve.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Not quite. A Skill can preserve the workflow, but this use case also needs to package the connected tools around it. That's where a Plugin fits.

blocks.text: Three Shapes a Skill Can Take
Skills can preserve different kinds of repeatable work:

• A process: Turn evidence into a promotion case, run a monthly review, prepare an executive brief.
  • A tool workflow: Gather the same information from connected sources and process it the same way each week.
  • A standard: Apply the same brand voice, report structure, or quality checks every time.
Naomi's weekly brief from the previous lessons could later become a tool-based Skill that applies the same retrieval and prioritization process each Monday.

Build a Skill when:
  • The task comes back repeatedly.
  • Good results depend on the same method.
  • The input changes, but the process stays stable.
  • Missing one step creates a meaningful problem.
A one-time question or a task that changes completely every time usually needs a good prompt, but not a new Skill.
blocks.title: 💡 When a Skill Is Worth Building

blocks.text: Where Skills Live
In the ChatGPT web interface, open Plugins on the left tab and select Skills. Today you'll create a personal Skill. Click "+" and choose one of the three options.
Three Ways to Create a Skill
You can create a new Skill using these methods:

• Create with chat: Describe the Skill in plain language and let ChatGPT guide you.
  • Create with editor: Write and edit the Skill structure directly.
  • Upload from your computer: Upload an existing Skill.
The first route is the simplest to begin with. It requires no technical setup and lets you develop the Skill through conversation.
Start Skill Creator

Once you choose "Create with chat," ChatGPT opens a guided creation conversation with a starter prompt. Send it, then describe the task you want the Skill to handle. The builder may ask follow-up questions about the trigger, inputs, workflow, output, and boundaries before preparing the first draft.
What Stays and What Changes
Your reusable Skill should keep the parts that stay stable:

• The evidence-review process
  • The attribution rules
  • The required output structure
  • The promotion framework, if it is the standard you want to reuse
The campaign report, experiment notes, and stakeholder feedback vary by review. Those are fresh inputs you provide when you run the Skill.

feedbackCorrect.text: The framework is a reusable reference that guides every review, so it belongs to the Skill.

feedbackIncorrect.text: This framework is part of the repeatable method, so keeping it with the Skill means the same evaluation standard can be applied to each new evidence pack.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Not quite. The report belongs to a specific review period, so it shouldn't be built into the reusable Skill. Supply each new campaign report when you run the Skill, while keeping the same review rules and output structure.

blocks.text: Let's Build Your Skill
Upload your documents and brief ChatGPT. A strong Skill brief defines:

• What goes in.
  • What process runs.
  • What must never happen.
  • What comes out.

blocks.exampleResponse:
Skill brief ready
  • Use for promotion evidence
  • Use supplied files only
  • Separate personal contribution from team results
  • Rate evidence as strong, partial, or missing
  • Flag unsupported claims
  • Return an evidence table and 3-5 statements
blocks.prompt: Complete the instructions for the Promotion Evidence Curator.
blocks.template:
Build a personal Skill called "Promotion Evidence Curator" for [scope]. Use only [source boundary].
For each achievement, separate [attribution] from team results, map it to the competency framework, and rate the evidence as strong, partial, or missing.
When the evidence is incomplete, [fallback instruction]. Return an evidence table and three to five review-ready statements.

blocks.text: Answer the Builder's Questions
Skill Creator may ask you to clarify:

• When should the Skill be used?
  • What files or information does it need?
  • Which steps must it follow?
  • What should the final result contain?
  • What must it never claim or invent?
For this Skill, make the central rule explicit: Surface my full documented contribution. Do not reduce specific analytical work to vague phrases.
Review Before You Install
Skill Creator prepares a draft and gives you the option to install it. Before selecting Install, check:

• Is the trigger specific?
  • Does it use only supplied evidence?
  • Does it separate individual work from team outcomes?
  • Does it include the evidence table and achievement statements?
  • Is the promotion framework included as a reference?
  • Are the practice campaign files excluded from the reusable Skill?
Ask ChatGPT to revise anything that's unclear before installing it.
Test the Skill in a New Chat

Start a new chat and upload a fresh evidence pack. Type "@" in the prompt bar and select Promotion Evidence Curator. Selecting the Skill explicitly makes testing easier. Later, ChatGPT may also choose it automatically when your request clearly matches its description. Then ask: "Review these files and build my promotion evidence table. Use only claims the files support."
The Skill first turns the files into an evidence row and then writes concluding evidence claims.
Now Test the Boundary
Nicely done! However, strong evidence is the easy case. The Skill also needs to behave correctly when the result is real, but the user's contribution isn't fully documented.

feedbackCorrect.text: The result itself is supported, so it can stay. What isn't supported is the claim that you personally caused it. A reliable Skill keeps the documented outcome while clearly flagging the missing attribution.

feedbackIncorrect.text: The evidence supports the 12% result, so removing it throws away valid information. But claiming you drove the increase goes too far. Keep the metric, separate it from personal ownership, and flag what the files don't prove.

options.label: Turn the result into a personal achievement and write, "Drove a 12% increase in conversion"
Remove the 12% result completely because the files don't fully prove personal ownership
Keep the 12% result as supported context, but flag that your personal contribution to it isn't fully documented

blocks.question: A second evidence pack shows that conversion increased by 12%, but none of the files proves that you caused the increase. What should the Skill do?

blocks.text: Fix the Skill, Not the One Answer

The second test exposed a gap in the Skill: it recognized the 12% result, but it still needs a clearer rule for separating a documented team outcome from an unsupported claim of personal ownership.

Instead of correcting only this answer, update the Skill so it handles the same evidence pattern correctly every time. Let's try it out!
To make targeted edits, find your Skill in the Skills library. Click Edit to adjust its workflow instructions and add the missing rule.

In the Editor, select SKILL.md — the main file that contains the Skill's reusable instructions and workflow rules. Find the section that explains how to assess results and personal contribution. Then add a rule that tells the Skill what to do when the files prove an outcome but not who caused it.

correctTokens: keep the result as supported team or project context
attribute the full result to the employee
blocks.prompt: Complete the editing instruction that prevents the Skill from turning a supported team result into an unsupported claim.
blocks.template: When the files support a measurable result but don't prove that the employee personally caused it, [supported treatment]. Do not [unsupported claim]. Instead, describe the documented personal contribution separately and flag the missing attribution evidence.
tokens: keep the result as supported team or project context
attribute the full result to the employee

blocks.text: The Skill Is Stronger Now
Nicely done! You found a recurring weakness and turned it into a clear rule. Don't forget to confirm that the Skill now handles the same evidence more reliably.

• Use a Skill when the method should stay consistent. It preserves a focused workflow, its rules, references, and required output.
  • Choose the right reusable feature. A Skill keeps one method; a Custom GPT creates a dedicated assistant; a Plugin can package the workflow with connected tools.
  • Define both the task and its boundaries. Specify what the Skill should produce, which sources it may use, and what it must never assume or invent.
  • Review and test before relying on it. Check the draft before installing, then test it on clear, partial, and ambiguous evidence.
  • Improve the reusable rule, not only one answer. When testing reveals a recurring weakness, edit SKILL.md, save the change, and run the same case again.

blocks.text: Build a Skill That Makes Your Work Count

Imagine a promotion review is approaching. You know you've done strong work — but the proof is scattered across reports, experiment notes, dashboards, and stakeholder feedback. In this lesson, you'll build a personal ChatGPT Skill that provides real proof of work and turns your strongest achievements into a promotion-ready evidence table. Let's get started!
The Promotion Case Hidden in Your Files
You're a marketing analyst preparing for promotion to a senior position. You have your key results scattered over four important files:

• A campaign performance report
  • An experiment summary
  • Stakeholder feedback
  • The company's promotion framework
The hard part is proving exactly what you contributed.
The Real Task Isn't Better Writing
A useful promotion case applies the same judgment to every achievement:

• Separate personal contribution from team results.
  • Preserve only metrics supported by the evidence.
  • Map each achievement to the relevant competency.
  • Rate the evidence and flag anything that remains unproven.
You could paste these rules into every new chat, or teach ChatGPT the process once.
The Missing Layer

In the previous lessons, you changed what ChatGPT could reach and do: you built a Custom GPT, connected an API, brought in external apps, and passed information between them. This task has a different problem. The tools are already there. What you need to preserve is the method: the same evidence rules, checks, and output structure every time a new promotion review comes around. That's where a Skill comes in.
Meet Skills
A Skill is a reusable workflow that tells ChatGPT how to handle a specific task consistently. It can keep:

• The steps ChatGPT should follow
  • The required output format
  • Examples, templates, and reference materials
  • Rules about what to include or avoid

Once installed, ChatGPT can automatically use a relevant Skill from the triggers. You can also choose it yourself with an "@" mention in ChatGPT Work, or explicitly mention the Skill you want to use in the prompt.
Why a Skill, Not Another Custom GPT?

A Custom GPT gives you a dedicated assistant for a broader role or use case. A Skill is different: it preserves one reusable method that ChatGPT can apply whenever that task comes up. In your case, every promotion review brings new evidence. But the way you evaluate that evidence stays the same. You need the same review method applied to each fresh evidence pack.

feedbackCorrect.text: A Skill fits because it's a focused method you want ChatGPT to apply whenever the same type of task comes up. It preserves the steps and standards without requiring a separate assistant.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Not quite. Custom GPT would create a dedicated assistant with its own broader setup. Here, you only need ChatGPT to reuse a specific review method, which is what a Skill is designed for.

Custom GPT

blocks.question: You want ChatGPT to apply the same evidence-review method whenever you assess a project update

blocks.text: A Skill or a Plugin?

You also used Plugins — installable packages that can include Skills, connected apps, or both — for workflows that imply connections to external services. For the promotion task, you don't need a new service. You need ChatGPT to apply the same evidence rules every time, so you'll create a Skill.

feedbackCorrect.text: A Plugin can package a workflow together with the apps or other capabilities it needs. A Skill is enough when the reusable method itself is the main thing you want to preserve.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Not quite. A Skill can preserve the workflow, but this use case also needs to package the connected tools around it. That's where a Plugin fits.

blocks.text: Three Shapes a Skill Can Take
Skills can preserve different kinds of repeatable work:

• A process: Turn evidence into a promotion case, run a monthly review, prepare an executive brief.
  • A tool workflow: Gather the same information from connected sources and process it the same way each week.
  • A standard: Apply the same brand voice, report structure, or quality checks every time.
Naomi's weekly brief from the previous lessons could later become a tool-based Skill that applies the same retrieval and prioritization process each Monday.

Build a Skill when:
  • The task comes back repeatedly.
  • Good results depend on the same method.
  • The input changes, but the process stays stable.
  • Missing one step creates a meaningful problem.
A one-time question or a task that changes completely every time usually needs a good prompt, but not a new Skill.

blocks.text: Where Skills Live
In the ChatGPT web interface, open Plugins on the left tab and select Skills. Today you'll create a personal Skill. Click "+" and choose one of the three options.
Three Ways to Create a Skill
You can create a new Skill using these methods:

• Create with chat: Describe the Skill in plain language and let ChatGPT guide you.
  • Create with editor: Write and edit the Skill structure directly.
  • Upload from your computer: Upload an existing Skill.
The first route is the simplest to begin with. It requires no technical setup and lets you develop the Skill through conversation.
Start Skill Creator

Once you choose "Create with chat," ChatGPT opens a guided creation conversation with a starter prompt. Send it, then describe the task you want the Skill to handle. The builder may ask follow-up questions about the trigger, inputs, workflow, output, and boundaries before preparing the first draft.
What Stays and What Changes
Your reusable Skill should keep the parts that stay stable:

• The evidence-review process
  • The attribution rules
  • The required output structure
  • The promotion framework, if it is the standard you want to reuse
The campaign report, experiment notes, and stakeholder feedback vary by review. Those are fresh inputs you provide when you run the Skill.

feedbackIncorrect.text: This framework is part of the repeatable method, so keeping it with the Skill means the same evaluation standard can be applied to each new evidence pack.

Upload your documents and brief ChatGPT. A strong Skill brief defines:

  • What must never happen.
  • What comes out.

blocks.text: Answer the Builder's Questions
Skill Creator may ask you to clarify:

• When should the Skill be used?
  • What files or information does it need?
  • Which steps must it follow?

  • What must it never claim or invent?
For this Skill, make the central rule explicit: Surface my full documented contribution. Do not reduce specific analytical work to vague phrases.
Review Before You Install
Skill Creator prepares a draft and gives you the option to install it. Before selecting Install, check:

• Is the trigger specific?
  • Does it use only supplied evidence?
  • Does it separate individual work from team outcomes?
  • Does it include the evidence table and achievement statements?
  • Is the promotion framework included as a reference?
  • Are the practice campaign files excluded from the reusable Skill?
Ask ChatGPT to revise anything that's unclear before installing it.
Test the Skill in a New Chat

Start a new chat and upload a fresh evidence pack. Type "@" in the prompt bar and select Promotion Evidence Curator. Selecting the Skill explicitly makes testing easier. Later, ChatGPT may also choose it automatically when your request clearly matches its description. Then ask: "Review these files and build my promotion evidence table. Use only claims the files support."

blocks.title: Key Takeaways

blocks.text: What's Next

First Unit Complete! 

The next stretch is about building. You'll start creating your own things in ChatGPT — generate consistent visual assets and campaigns, build vibe-coded projects that go from a plain-language description to a working tool. And you'll use ChatGPT Work and Codex to set up even more automated routines.

Let's keep going!
Create a Consistent Image Set

You've likely made single images before: created a scene, an illustration, or a quick graphic. This lesson goes a step deeper: making a set of images in the same style and colors that look like they belong together. You'll build the full look for an event and keep it consistent across every piece. Let's get started!
Scenario: A Workshop You're Running
Imagine this: you're running a one-day film photography workshop — Shoot & Develop at Northframe Studio. It needs three different pieces that have to feel like the same event:

• A poster for the wall
  • A post for Instagram
  • A ticket for everyone who signs up
The hard part is making all three share the same colors, style, and instructor's face, so they read as a coherent campaign. That consistency is the skill you'll build in this lesson.
The Image Workspace
Open ChatGPT's image tool and you'll see a single prompt box with a row of ready-made ideas underneath. Scroll across, and you'll find a whole set to browse.
A Preset Worth Using

Those presets are real shortcuts. You tap the shortcut, and it lets you create finished, polished visuals from a single preset prompt and an image you upload. Handwritten style, for instance, takes one of your own pictures and lays it out like a poster, with hand-lettered captions scattered across it — the kind of warm, personal styling that isn't far from what an event poster wants.
Where a Preset Stops

A preset is a strong starting point, and you can edit its prompt to make the image look the way you want. But it's built for a single, personal image — not for maintaining a consistent look across the image set.

The more your real goal differs from the preset's purpose, the more you're rewriting anyway. For a campaign, it's cleaner to write your own from the start.

feedbackCorrect.text: Right on! A preset hands you a look, but a matched set carrying your exact date and price needs your own prompt — that's where you take control.

feedbackIncorrect.text: A preset can't carry your specific date and price, or hold one identity across three pieces. It shines for a quick standalone image, not a matched set.

blocks.instruction: Decide whether a one-tap preset is enough for this job, or if you need your own prompt.

options.label: A preset
Your own prompt

blocks.question: A set of three event pieces that must share one identity and show the exact date and price

blocks.text: Define the Identity First

Consistency starts before you generate anything — by deciding the look you'll reuse. If you're not sure what that should be, ChatGPT can help you brainstorm it: describe the event and ask for a few distinct visual directions, then pick one to commit to.

correctTokens: with a style, a color palette, and a mood
blocks.exampleResponse: 1. Darkroom Minimal Style: Clean, editorial, black-and-white layouts with subtle grain and contact-sheet details Palette: Charcoal, warm white, soft gray, muted red Mood: Focused, intimate, craft-driven 2. Golden Hour Nostalgia Style: Soft vintage photography aesthetic, faded textures, handwritten notes, warm film borders Palette: Honey yellow, burnt orange, cream, dusty brown Mood: Warm, personal, reflective 3. Analog Street Style: Bold urban zine look, cropped photos, stickers, rough typography, flash-photo energy Palette: Black, off-white, cobalt blue, neon green or red accent Mood: Playful, spontaneous, creative chaos Recommended: Golden Hour Nostalgia
blocks.prompt: Complete the prompt that asks ChatGPT to propose visual directions before you generate.
blocks.template: I'm designing the look for [event]. Suggest [number] distinct visual directions — each [identity elements] — that would feel right for a film photography workshop. Keep them short so I can pick one.
tokens: with a style, a color palette, and a mood

blocks.text: Lock It In
From the directions ChatGPT offers, you go with the recommended Golden Hour Nostalgia:

• A soft vintage photography look
  • Faded textures
  • Handwritten notes
  • Warm film borders
  • A palette of honey yellow, burnt orange, cream, and dusty brown
  • The instructor as the consistent face for the campaign
When choosing the visual direction, save the details, as you'll reuse the suggested words across all visual assets.
Build It in Order
Build the set one piece at a time. Start with the anchor piece, refine it, then use its visual direction to guide the rest. Let's put the steps in order!

correctItems: Define the visual identity you'll reuse
Generate the poster as the anchor piece
Proofread the text and lock the version you like
Reuse that identity for the post and the ticket
Review all three side by side for drift

blocks.prompt: Arrange the steps to build a set of images that share a single identity.
blocks.title: The Order of a Consistent Set

blocks.text: Start With the Anchor

The poster is your anchor. It sets the visual direction for the entire set, so the other pieces will follow its style. 

It's also the most demanding: it has a lot of text, demands a clear layout, and includes a real photo of a person. That combination is where a slower, more deliberate mode pays off.
The Intelligence Level

Next to the prompt box, an effort dropdown lets you choose the Intelligence level — Instant, Medium, High. Instant is quick. Medium and High spend more time planning the composition, which holds up better for posters and other structured designs.

The instructor should be the same person in every piece, not a new stranger each time. To pin that down, upload a real photo of them and add the line "keep facial features exactly." From there, the same face carries across the poster, the post, and the ticket.
Set the Shape
One more choice before you generate: the aspect ratio. Include the required ratio directly in the prompt. For a poster, you pick Portrait 3:4, which closely matches the shape of a printed poster.

Images are rendered at screen resolution, which is fine on a phone or laptop but too light for large print. To print a poster at full size:
  • Generate at the highest available quality, in the correct aspect ratio.
  • For anything bigger than a sheet of paper, run the result through an image upscaler before printing — it adds the pixels a sharp, large print needs.
blocks.title: 💡 Generating for Print

correctTokens: a poster for a film photography workshop
honey yellow, cream, and dusty brown
blocks.prompt: Complete the prompt that generates the campaign's anchor piece.
blocks.template:
Create [visual asset]. Show the instructor in a darkroom developing a print, in a soft vintage photography style: faded texture, a warm film border, a handwritten note in the margin. Keep facial features exactly as in the reference picture. *Pasted reference picture*
Use [color palette] with burnt orange as the accent.
Include this text exactly, [lettering rule]: "Shoot & Develop", "One-Day Film Workshop", "June 14, 10 a.m.-5 p.m.", "Northframe Studio", "$90"
tokens: a poster for a film photography workshop
honey yellow, cream, and dusty brown

blocks.text:
Across the prompts for all the images from the set, these tips will help you:
  • Choose the format and shape — the medium and aspect ratio.
  • Describe composition, lighting, and style with concrete words.
  • Use a higher Intelligence level for text-heavy or structured layouts, and Instant for quick, simple images.
blocks.title: 💡 What Makes an Image Prompt Work

blocks.text: Proofread Before You Reuse

The poster comes back looking sharp — but read every word before you do anything else. Check the workshop name, date, time, and price. 

Text rendering is strong but not flawless, so an incorrect start time is cheap to fix here but costly after it's printed.
Carry the Brand, Not the Whole Look

The post has to read as the same campaign, but it doesn't have to copy the poster. What carries a brand across formats is the palette and the instructor's face, not an identical layout. 

So this time you'll keep those two fixed — palette and face — and deliberately change the style. You still feed the poster in as a reference — you just tell ChatGPT what to keep and what to change.

feedbackCorrect.text: That's right! The palette, the locked face, and the anchor reference are what the eye reads as "same campaign." Lock those, and each piece is free to suit its own format.

feedbackIncorrect.text: An identical layout feels safe, but a wall poster and a phone-feed post have different jobs. Forcing them to match flattens both — the palette and face carry the brand, not a copied layout.

options.label: A shared color palette across every piece
An identical layout and style on all three
The same locked instructor's face throughout
The anchor image fed in as a reference

blocks.question: What keeps a set looking like one campaign, even when the pieces aren't identical?

blocks.text: Continue in the same chat so that ChatGPT can use the visual direction, the original portrait, and the approved poster from the earlier steps. For each new asset, attach the relevant references and restate what must stay consistent.
blocks.title: 💡 Consistency Tip

blocks.prompt: In the same chat, complete the prompt that creates an Instagram post.
blocks.template:
Using the poster for the palette and the same instructor (keep the face exactly), create [output] in a different [style direction]: heavy hand-lettering, a bold layout, a smaller photo.
Keep the [color palette] palette, but make it hand-made rather than photographic.
Include only: "Shoot & Develop", "Sat June 14", "[Call to action]".

blocks.text: What Has to Stay the Same
Put the poster and the post side by side. The styles should look different — that's the point — so check the two things that must hold:

• Did the palette stay honey and burnt-orange?
  • Is it the same face?
If either slipped, fix that one piece against the poster rather than accepting a set that only half-matches.

When a piece is mostly right but one detail is off — the color drifted, a word is misspelled, the face changed — you don't regenerate the whole image. Describe just the change: "keep everything the same, only correct the date to June 16." The model edits that element and leaves the rest intact, so you don't lose the version you already liked.
A Ticket People Can Scan
The ticket has another feature: a QR code that links to the sign-up page. ChatGPT can build working, scannable code directly into the design, styled to match the rest of the set.

blocks.prompt: Complete the prompt for the third piece — a ticket with a scannable code.
blocks.template:
Using the poster as a style reference, create [output] in the same look. *Pasted image*
Include the text "Shoot & Develop", "June 14", "Admit One", and [detail] that links to *website link*. Keep the burnt orange accent.

blocks.text: Scan It Yourself
Before the ticket goes anywhere, point your phone camera at the code and confirm that it opens the correct page.

A matched set comes from a few deliberate moves:
  • Define the identity once: Style, palette, accent, and the recurring face.
  • Anchor first: Build the strongest piece, then copy its look.
  • Reference, don't re-describe: Feed the anchor image into each new piece.
  • Check for drift: Review the set together and fix any piece that wanders.
blocks.title: 💡 Designing as a Set

blocks.text: What's Still Your Call
The model handles the production, but the judgment stays with you:

• Whether the look fits the audience.
  • Whether it feels like Northframe.
  • Whether the message lands.
Keep it honest, too — don't have it generate real brand logos or trademarks you don't own.
The Finished Set
Look what you've got! You created three pieces that read as one campaign:

• A poster for the wall
  • A bolder hand-lettered version for Instagram
  • A ticket with a working code.
Now Shoot & Develop looks like a real event!

• Consistency is the real skill: Making several images share a single identity is harder and more useful than making one good image.
  • Define the identity, then anchor: Set your style, palette, accent, and face once; build the strongest piece first; then copy its look.
  • Reference the anchor and restate the constants: Feed the anchor image into each new piece, and lock the person with an uploaded photo.
  • Lock the constants, vary the rest: A shared palette and a single face carry a campaign even when a piece changes style to suit its format.
  • Verify what you ship: Proofread rendered text, scan the QR, and check the set for drift before it goes out.
  • Presets start, you finish: A preset is a fast way to find a look; your own prompts carry it across a set with your exact text.
blocks.title: Key Takeaways

blocks.text: What's Next?
Great job! Now you have a consistent visual campaign for your event. In the next lesson, you'll build something new: a website described in plain language. Let's keep going!

Build and Publish a Live Site

You've built a consistent visual campaign for Northframe Studio. Now it needs somewhere to send people — a website where visitors can see the work, explore the packages, and submit a booking request. With ChatGPT Sites, you can describe that experience, review the result, refine it, and publish it without setting up separate hosting. Let's get started!
From Prompt to Live Site

A website usually means choosing a builder, setting up hosting, and publishing the result. Sites brings those steps into one ChatGPT workflow: you describe what you want, and ChatGPT builds it, hosts it, and hands you a link. Let's turn that into something real!
What's a Site?

A Site is a hosted website, web app, or game that ChatGPT creates and runs for you. You don't need to set up separate tools to get it online — you prompt ChatGPT, it creates and hosts the experience, and you can reopen, refine, and share it any time from the Sites view. Sites are available on paid plans through More → Sites. You can also access it anytime by adding @Sites to your request in Work mode.
Scenario: The Studio Without a Website

You run a small photography studio. Booking inquiries arrive through direct messages, comments, and a notebook — and details keep slipping: which Saturday, which package, indoor or outdoor? You've wanted a real website for years, but the tool stack always stopped you.

What you need is one page that shows your work and packages, plus a form where visitors can submit their name, contact details, and all the important shoot details.

The site also needs to save each request and give you a private place to review the submitted forms. Before Sites, building this flow meant hiring a developer and combining several tools. Now it starts with one clear request.
Writing the Request
A working Sites request names the following things:

• Audience: Who uses it?
  • Purpose: What should the visitors accomplish?
  • Content: What should they see?
  • Behavior: What should happen when they interact?
  • Data: What must remain saved?

Show a portfolio gallery and package prices using the uploaded campaign assets *uploaded assets*. Let visitors [core experience] with their name, email, [data], location, shoot type, and a reference photo, and get a confirmation message.

blocks.text: A Question Before the Build

Site doesn't always start building right away — it comes back with a question and a few named styles, each rendered as a live preview. Look at what just happened: your brief named the audience, the experience, and the information, and the look was the one thing it left open. ChatGPT asks about that gap.

Suppose you pick Cinematic Editorial — the minimal that reads as premium. It supports your package prices. ChatGPT builds the site and returns a private preview where you can edit right away if something feels off.

The first preview gives you a working direction, not a finished Site yet.

Now review it: first as a potential client submitting a request, then as the studio owner.

The site looks good, but the package prices are buried below the gallery. Instead of rebuilding, describe the changes in the Edit panel: "Move the packages above the gallery." Then review the updated preview again.
Look What You've Built
Now that your site looks polished, you can proceed to test the booking flow. You start filling in the form, and something doesn't work as you intended.

feedbackCorrect.text: Exactly! The form accepted the request, but the Site wasn't told to keep the data. Persistent storage ensures that submissions remain available after the page is closed or refreshed.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Not quite. A confirmation message and visitor sign-in don't make submissions persistent. Persistent storage ensures that submissions remain available after the page is closed or refreshed. The build must explicitly keep the booking records between visits.

blocks.text: A form can look completely functional even while the details behind it disappear the moment a visitor refreshes or closes your Site. If booking requests, uploaded files, or saved progress need to still be there later, say so right in your prompt: "Keep this data saved between visits."

blocks.text: Test the Full Booking Flow
Great! Now, with this fix implemented, test the full flow. Submit a test request as a client would. Then check:

• Does the form require the essential fields?
  • Does the confirmation appear?
  • Is the request still available after you reopen the site?
  • Can the studio owner find the saved request?
Fix anything that breaks before saving a version.
One Step Before It Goes Live
The Site is still in preview, so clients can't open it yet. Before publishing, save a reviewable version and check the complete experience one last time.
Sites publishing has two separate stages:

1. Save a version that builds a reviewable candidate.
  2. Deploy a version that publishes it and reports the production URL.
You deploy only when clients should actually reach the site.
Once you deploy the Site, people with access can open it through the link. Save and review the latest version first, then deploy when it's ready to share.
blocks.title: 💡 Deployment Makes the URL Live

blocks.text: Who Can Open It

Hosting a Site doesn't automatically make it public. Depending on your account and workspace settings, you can choose the audience: only you and people you invite, everyone in your workspace, or anyone with the link.

To share the website, click "Share" and choose "Anyone with the link."

Sharing lets people visit the Site — it doesn't let them edit it. Keep passwords and secret keys out of prompts and page content, and remember that Sites must not handle payment card details or health data — your form takes booking requests, and deposits stay in the channel you already use.

feedbackCorrect.text: Behavior, content, and access — that's the review. A link-shared Site reaches the people you send it to.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Being findable sounds like a win, but a link-shared Site reaches clients through the link you distribute — your bio, messages, a QR code. Search visibility isn't a readiness check. The review is behavior, content, and access.

content.value: Who Can Open It

Hosting a Site doesn't automatically make it public. Depending on your account and workspace settings, you can choose the audience: only you and people you invite, everyone in your workspace, or anyone with the link.

To share the website, click "Share" and choose "Anyone with the link."
https://d2h7i1o4snhir4.cloudfront.net/page-fragments/b3da1943-2f9e-432d-92a1-87f69fe383e0.jpg

Sharing lets people visit the Site — it doesn't let them edit it. Keep passwords and secret keys out of prompts and page content, and remember that Sites must not handle payment card details or health data — your form takes booking requests, and deposits stay in the channel you already use.

feedback_correct.text: Behavior, content, and access — that's the review. A link-shared Site reaches the people you send it to.

feedback_incorrect.text: Being findable sounds like a win, but a link-shared Site reaches clients through the link you distribute — your bio, messages, a QR code. Search visibility isn't a readiness check. The review is behavior, content, and access.

options.text: Open the Site the way a client would and confirm the gallery, the form, and the photo upload behave as expected
Check that nothing ended up in the content that shouldn't be public — client photos without permission, personal notes, anything you didn't mean to publish
Confirm the access setting matches the audience you actually intend

blocks.text: What's Next?

Build an App Just by Describing It

Imagine describing an app in plain words — what it does, how it looks — and watching a working version appear a few seconds later without writing a single line of code on your side. That's vibe coding, and in this lesson, you'll use it to build something for a friend that no store could sell. Let's get started!
A Gift You Can't Buy

Imagine this: your best friend Marta has a birthday coming up. Instead of buying another gift, you decide to make something personal — a small game filled with your shared memories, inside jokes, and moments only the two of you would recognize.

The catch? You've never built an app before. That's where vibe coding comes in.
What's Vibe Coding?

Vibe coding means describing what you want in plain language and letting AI write the code behind it. You type a description, ChatGPT builds the app, shows it running, and you refine it through plain-language iterations. The real skill here isn't coding but precisely describing and judging what comes back.
Build The Game With Sites

In the previous lesson, you used Sites to build a website. Now you'll use it to make an interactive game. The Sites feature creates a private preview where you can play through the game, describe changes, and review each new version. The game stays in the Sites view, so you can reopen it, refine it, and publish a link when it is ready for Marta.
Brief It Before You Build
Building an app starts with the brief: you define what you want before it runs. A solid app brief names four things:

• The user of the app
  • The core function the app performs
  • The key interactions the user has with it
  • The scope cutoff: what you leave out on purpose
The clearer you get, the closer the first build comes back.

pairs.left: User
pairs.right: Marta, opening it on her phone on her birthday

pairs.left: Core function
pairs.right: A game that quizzes her on your friendship and scores it

pairs.left: Key interactions
pairs.right: Tapping answers, dragging a slider, seeing her result

pairs.left: Scope cutoff
pairs.right: One self-contained page — no logins, nothing saved to an account

blocks.prompt: Match each part of the app brief to its meaning for Marta's game.
blocks.title: Brief the Birthday Game

blocks.text: The Game's Flow
After the briefing, you start outlining the game structure and thinking of the screens you want to add. Let's arrange the game's screen in the correct sequence.

Ask a question about your friendship
Check whether her answer is right
Light a candle on the cake for a correct answer
After the last question, reveal a birthday message

blocks.title: Build the Game's Core Flow

blocks.text: When proceeding to the building, don't ask for the whole game at once. Build the smallest version that runs end-to-end — the core loop — and confirm it works before adding anything.
blocks.title: Start With the Core Loop

blocks.text: For Marta, the core loop is plain:

• A welcome screen with her name
  • Five multiple-choice questions about your friendship
  • A running score and a final tally
No cake, no confetti yet — just the working loop. Let's build it!

blocks.prompt: Complete the prompt that builds the first working version of Marta's game.

blocks.text: It Runs — Now Make It a Game
Great job! The loop works: welcome screen, five questions, a score at the end. But it doesn't feel like a game yet. Once the core loop works, that's the next step.
Quiz Versus Game
Three things separate a quiz from a game:

• Stakes the player can see
  • Variety in how rounds play
  • A payoff for finishing
For Marta, that's a birthday cake whose candles light as she scores, one round that swaps buttons for a number slider, and a personal message that appears at the end.
How to Iterate Without Breaking It
From here, you grow the game by talking, and a few habits keep that from going sideways:

• Change one thing per prompt, so when something breaks, you know the cause.
  • Test each change before asking for the next.
  • When a version works well, tell ChatGPT to keep it as a fixed point you can return to if a later change makes things worse.

blocks.prompt: Complete the prompt that adds stakes, variety, and a payoff in one batch of related changes.
blocks.template:
Add a birthday cake that gains a lit candle [condition], shown after every question and again on the results screen.
Replace one question with a round where Marta [action] — "How many cups of tea does Marta drink a day?" — and count it correct if the number is 4.
When she reaches the end, [payoff] with a short confetti animation. Keep the same warm style and the single file.

blocks.text: Now Test It

Good job! You applied the iteration rules, and the app looks polished. Now it's time for testing. Play it through, and it feels finished — cake, slider, confetti, a message at the end. But running without errors isn't the same as working correctly. 

Before this becomes a gift, make sure everything works correctly and check it the way a developer would.
What QA Means
QA, or quality assurance, is the deliberate practice of checking that software does what it's meant to — not just that it opens. Developers never ship without it.

The first check: try something you know the answer to. Answer one question wrong on purpose, then watch the results screen. If the cake still lights every candle and the message still appears, the logic is wrong — the app is rewarding answers it shouldn't.

The second check: after each change, retest what worked before. Adding the slider round may have changed how the score is counted, so the cake no longer fills even on a perfect game. A new change breaking old behavior is the most common — and most missed — failure in vibe coding.

The third check: open it as someone who's never seen it. You built it, so every button is obvious to you — but Marta doesn't know the game's logic you thought of. What's clear to the builder may not be that clear to the player.

pairs.left: The cake lights every candle even when an answer was wrong
pairs.right: Logic that rewards answers it shouldn't

pairs.left: Adding the slider stopped the score from counting the other rounds
pairs.right: A new change that broke the earlier behavior

pairs.left: Marta opens it and isn't sure how to start
pairs.right: A screen that's clear to you but not to her

blocks.prompt: Match each QA check to the kind of failure it's built to catch.
blocks.title: Match the Check to the Catch

blocks.text: Describe What's Wrong, Precisely
When a check turns up a problem, the fix depends on how well you describe it. Give ChatGPT three things:

• What you did
  • What happened
  • What should have happened instead

blocks.exampleResponse: Found it — the score was treating every answered question as correct. Fixed: a candle lights only for a correct answer, and the message appears only at a full score. Answer one wrong in the preview now — the cake should come up one candle short, and the message should stay hidden.
blocks.prompt: Complete the message that tells ChatGPT exactly what to fix.
blocks.template:
A bug to fix. What I did: I answered one question [condition].
What happened: the cake [observation], and the message still appeared.
What should happen: a wrong answer [expected behavior], and the message should appear only on a full score.

blocks.text:
A preview that looks right isn't proof that it works. Run these three checks, then report precisely on anything you vibe code:
  • Test a standard flow to catch logic that's quietly wrong.
  • Re-test after each change to catch new edits breaking old behavior.
  • Watch a first-timer to catch what's clear to you but not to them.
  • Report precisely what you did, what happened, and what should have happened.
blocks.title: 💡 QA Before You Ship

blocks.text: Save the Finished Version
Once the game passes your tests, save a version. This gives you a reviewable candidate. Open it and play through it one last time before publishing.
Publish It for Marta
Choose who should be able to open the game, then deploy the approved version as you did in the previous lesson. Sites creates a link, and you can add it to Marta's birthday message!
But open the published link yourself first and confirm that the game works outside the preview.
Marta Plays It

Marta taps the link on her birthday. Her name and a burst of confetti, then your five questions, the candles lighting one by one, and the message you wrote waiting at the end. You built it in an afternoon, from a handful of sentences.

• Vibe coding turns a plain-language description into a working app: The skill is describing precisely and judging the result, not writing code.
  • Brief it in four parts: The user, core function, key interactions, scope cutoff — then build the core loop before anything else.
  • Iterate in control. One change per prompt, test each before the next, and keep a known-good version to fall back to.
  • QA before you ship: Test a known case, re-test after each change, watch a first-timer, and report bugs precisely.

blocks.text: What's Next?

You turned a sentence into a working app — one kind of creative project you can make in ChatGPT. Next, you'll meet Codex — an AI agent that lives in the files on your computer — and complete the tasks that were too overwhelming to even think about. Let's keep going!

blocks.text: What's Next?

You turned a sentence into a working app — one kind of creative project you can make in ChatGPT. Next, you'll meet Codex — an AI agent that lives in the files on your computer — and complete the tasks that were too overwhelming to even think about. Let's keep going!
The Work You Keep Putting Off

There's always that one task you've been meaning to do for weeks. The folder you keep meaning to organize. The list you keep meaning to clean up. Work that's simple to describe and miserable to do by hand, so it never gets done. In this lesson, you'll use ChatGPT Work to handle a long, repetitive task across files on your computer — and learn how to keep the result safe and reviewable. Let's start!
The Task You'd Never Do by Hand

Imagine this: 12K photos in one folder, collected over 8 years. Then there are 500 contacts spread across three exports, full of duplicates and inconsistent formatting. The work's easy to describe and miserable to complete one file at a time. This lesson is about handing these tasks to ChatGPT Work while keeping control over what it changes.
Meet ChatGPT Work
The ChatGPT desktop app brings three experiences into one place:

• Chat for work that you guide through conversation: exploring ideas, producing content, analyzing files.
  • Work for longer tasks that involve several steps, files, tools, and finished outputs.
  • Codex for complex workflows, software development, repositories, and tests. You'll explore it in the next lesson.
When to Use Work, Chat, or Codex
So, when is it best to use each experience?

• Use Chat when you want to explore an idea, analyze information, or create something through conversation.
  • Use Work when you want ChatGPT to complete a longer task across files or tools on your computer and return a finished result.
  • Use Codex when the task involves complex workflows, building, testing, or reviewing software.
Your task is file cleanup, so in this lesson, you'll use Work.

Work is built for tasks that involve several steps and a concrete outcome to review at the end. In the desktop app, it can use a folder you select, inspect and edit files inside that workspace, and create new outputs for you to review.
Web or Desktop?
You can use Work on the web or in the ChatGPT desktop app. For this lesson, you'll need the desktop app so ChatGPT can access the files stored on your computer.
Desktop Work can open a folder on your device and work directly with its files. On the web, you can work with files you upload manually.
Start Your Work Session
Open the ChatGPT desktop app and select ChatGPT in the top-left mode switcher. Then, choose the Work mode. You can start a standalone task or create a project.
Project or Standalone Task?
A standalone task works for a quick, self-contained job. Create a project when:

• Several tasks use the same files
  • You want to return to work later
  • The outputs should stay together
  • The task may eventually repeat
Your First Task: 8 Years of Photos
Remember the photo dump with 12K photos that you need to sort? Filenames like "IMG_4471.jpg" tell you nothing. You want them renamed by the date each was taken, sorted into folders by year and month.
Create the Photo Project

Create a local project called Photo Cleanup. To do so, click the + next to Projects, then choose Work in a folder, and select the one with your files, containing a copy of the photo library. A local project gives Work access to the selected folder, while keeping the task focused on those files only. Don't begin with the originals, so you can test renaming and sorting safely. If the rules need adjusting, your original library stays untouched.
To complete your first task, you want Work to read the available data, propose clearer filenames, and organize the copies into folders by year and month.
What a Good Brief Needs
Define five things before Work changes anything:

• Goal = what you want done
  • Input = which files and in what format
  • Output = what the result should look like
  • Fallback = what to do when something doesn't fit the pattern
  • Review point = what it must show you before the full run
Skip the fallback, and Work makes its own call when it hits a file that doesn't fit — and you won't know it happened.

correctTokens: sort them into year and month folders
blocks.exampleResponse: Task understood. Here's the plan before I run: — Rename: each photo to its capture date from the photo's metadata (format: YYYY-MM-DD) — Sort: into folders by year, then by month — Fallback: any photo with no date metadata → moved to "Needs Review" rather than renamed I'll run this on a small sample first so you can confirm before I process all 12K. Proceed?

blocks.template: Rename every photo in this folder by [input source], then [output structure]. If a photo [fallback condition], move it to a "Needs Review" folder.

blocks.text: Don't Run It on All 12K Yet
Notice what Work offered at the end: a sample first. That's the single most important habit with any agent that acts on real files.

feedbackCorrect.text: A sample is a cheap test. If the naming or sorting logic is off, you find out after 20 files — not after the agent has renamed your entire library the wrong way.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Work handles large batches fine, and sampling doesn't speed up the total job. The point is safety: verify the logic on a small set before committing to an action that's tedious to undo at scale.

options.label: Because Work can't process 12K files at once
To make the task run faster overall
To catch a mistake at 20 files instead of after it's hit all 12K

blocks.question: Why run Work on a 20-photo sample before the full amount?

blocks.text: Before you let it loose on 12K photos, you check it on 20. If the sample comes back right, the full run is safe. If it doesn't, you've caught the problem at 20 files instead of 12K.
The Sample Looks Right — Run It

The 20 sample photos come back correctly renamed and sorted. The date logic works, the folders are right, and nothing landed in "Needs Review" that shouldn't have.

Now you authorize the full run. Work processes all 12K and saves them to your folder.
The One-Time Cleanup Is Done!

The folder is organized, but new photos will keep arriving. Instead of letting another eight-year folder build up, you can schedule a task to sort your photos automatically. Let's do it using the "Scheduled" feature.
Scheduled lets ChatGPT run a task later without waiting for you to start it manually. A task can:

• Run once at a chosen time.
  • Repeat on a schedule.
  • Return to an existing Work task and reuse its context.
  • Check for changes regularly and report when something relevant happens.
For the photo workflow, you'll create a monthly task that returns to the setup you've already tested.

Create an "Incoming" folder inside the project folder on your computer. New files go there first. Next, schedule the new routine from the current Work task so it returns to the same project and reuses the approved rules.

Stay inside the Work task where you tested the photo workflow. In the composer, type: "Schedule this workflow for the first Saturday of every month at 10 a.m. Return to this task each time and reuse the approved rules. Process only the Incoming folder." Send the message and review the proposed schedule.
Then open the scheduled task from the conversation or in the "Scheduled" section in the left sidebar. There, you can navigate the existing tasks and add more. Review the task and edit it if needed.
Great Job!
On the first Saturday of each month, Work checks the "Incoming" folder and runs the same sorting workflow. Now, everything is organized from a single prompt and a small automation.
A Messier Job — 500 Contacts

The photo task was clean: every photo has a date, and the rule is unambiguous. But some file work isn't that tidy.

Picture your contacts: exported from your phone, your email, and an old spreadsheet. A lot of rows, full of duplicates, inconsistent formatting, and half-empty fields. You want one clean list — but "clean" here involves judgment the photo task never did.
Where Judgment Comes In

Renaming a photo by its date yields a single correct answer. Merging contacts doesn't. Is "Jon Smith" the same person as "Jonathan Smith"? Is the same email under two different names one contact or two? Work has to make calls like these — and if you don't tell it how, it decides on its own, and you won't see what it chose.

feedbackCorrect.text: The photo rule was mechanical — date in, folder out. Merging means deciding when two near-matches are really one person. That ambiguity is exactly where your brief has to give Work a rule.

feedbackIncorrect.text: File size isn't the issue, and Work reads spreadsheets well. The difficulty is judgment: near-duplicate entries have no obvious right answer, so Work needs you to define how to handle the uncertain cases.

options.label: Contact files are larger than photo files — the bigger the file, the harder it is to process
Merging requires judgment calls — when two entries might be the same person, there's no single right answer
Work can't read spreadsheets; it only works with images and text

blocks.question: Merging the contact list is harder for Work than renaming photos. Why?

blocks.text: Briefing for the Uncertain Cases
This is where the fallback earns its place. For the contacts, the fallback isn't "set it aside" — it's a rule for what counts as a match and what to do when Work isn't sure.

correctTokens: the name and email both match
blocks.exampleResponse: Plan before running: — Combine: all three sources into one list, standardize formatting (names, phone, email) — Merge: two entries only when name and email match — Uncertain cases: near-matches (same name, different email; or same email, different name) → flagged in a separate "Review" tab, not merged Found 42 clear duplicates and 8 uncertain pairs. Want me to run the 42 clear merges and flag the 8 for you?
blocks.prompt: Work has access to the project folder with your three contact exports. Complete the brief to merge them and flag uncertainties.
blocks.template: Combine all three files into one list and [command]. Merge two entries only when [merge condition]. When you're not sure they're the same person, [fallback action] instead of merging.
tokens: the name and email both match

blocks.text: The Difference a Fallback Makes

Great job! Without that rule, Work would have merged every near-match on its own, quietly collapsing two real people into one.

With it, you get 492 safe merges handled automatically and 8 judgment calls returned to you. The agent does the bulk work; you make only the decisions that actually need a human.
Beyond Photos and Contacts
The same pattern fits any repetitive file job:

• 200 PDF receipts → one spreadsheet with date, vendor, amount
  • A folder of documents → renamed and sorted by content
  • Three messy exports → one clean, deduplicated list
Every single one is the same shape: point Work at the files, write the five-part brief, test on a sample, run. The task changes; the method doesn't.
What Work Reaches

That workspace you set up earlier — the project pointed at your folder — works because Work has something a chat doesn't: permission to your computer. It runs inside an environment tied to a folder of your files — read them, edit them, save new ones.
That's why the photos and contacts task worked. The files weren't somewhere on the web for an agent to reach through an API. They were on your machine. Work is the one with permission to be there.

• Use Work for longer, multi-step tasks across files that produce a finished result you can review.
  • A project keeps related files, instructions, and outputs together and gives Work access to the selected folder.
  • Brief file tasks in five parts: goal, input, output, fallback, and review point.
  • Work on copies and test the rules on a small sample before applying them to the full set.
  • Use a fallback to separate uncertain files or records instead of letting Work guess.
  • Once a workflow works reliably, use Scheduled to repeat it from the same Work task.

blocks.title: One Thing About Computer Use

blocks.text: Scenario: The Job Search You Need to Track

Imagine you're job-searching. Applications go out, recruiter emails come in, interview confirmations land, and follow-ups need to be sent. You meant to keep a record in a spreadsheet.

Two weeks in, the spreadsheet is half-empty, and you can't remember whether you replied to the last recruiter. By the end of this lesson, the spreadsheet will build itself every Friday, while you'll be doing something else.
Getting Started
Create a local project for the job search and link it to the folder with your tracker. This folder serves as the workspace for the spreadsheet and any downloaded attachments.
Connecting Gmail

Let's now connect the plugins. You've already met them in the previous lessons. In your new Codex local project with the spreadsheet in the folder, open the Plugins panel from the sidebar and find Gmail. Click Install, sign in, and approve the permissions that Codex requests. The connection stays put. Next time you assign a task involving email, Codex already has access without re-uploading or re-explaining.

feedbackCorrect.text: A plugin can package apps and Skills. The app provides access to current external data, while an upload is a fixed copy of information supplied to one task.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Installing a plugin does not necessarily make the connection exclusive to one local project. Access is governed by the underlying app connection and workspace permissions.

options.label: A plugin belongs only to the current project folder
A plugin may also include reusable workflow instructions
A plugin can use a connected app to access current information

blocks.question: What is the difference between a plugin and an uploaded email export?

blocks.text: A Workflow With Stages
A job search is a chain of steps, where each one feeds the next. Here's the chain you're going to build:

1. Gather: Pull this week's job-related emails from Gmail.
  2. Extract: Figure out the status for each company (applied, interviewing, rejected).
  3. File: Save attached PDFs to a company-named folder.
  4. Update: Add or change rows in the tracker spreadsheet.
  5. Flag: Surface threads that haven't moved in 14 days.
Each step depends on the one before it. Codex runs the whole chain in one go. Your job is to brief it well.
Write the Brief

With Gmail connected and the five stages clear, you write the whole chain as one brief — each stage named in order, so Codex runs them in sequence. Point it at the tracker file by its path so it updates the right spreadsheet, and spell out the flag rule at the end.

correctTokens: surface any thread silent for 14+ days
blocks.exampleResponse: Chain complete. Here's what ran: — Gathered 23 emails this week across 9 companies — Extracted statuses: Acme (interviewing), Northframe (applied), Velmix (offer received), Celqo (rejected), 1 new application. — Filed 11 PDFs into /JobSearch/{Company}/ (resumes confirmed, 2 take-home tasks, 3 offer letters). — Updated /JobSearch/tracker.xlsx: 1 new row added, 8 existing rows updated with current status. — Flagged for follow-up: 3 threads silent for 14+ days — Acme (last contact Nov 4), Prolvex (last contact Nov 6), Velmix (offer pending response since Nov 8). Open the tracker to see the full update.
blocks.prompt: Complete the stages of the brief.
blocks.template:
Pull this week's job-related emails from Gmail. For each company, [command] using one of: applied, interviewing, offer received, or rejected.
Save relevant attachments to /JobSearch/Company_name/.
Update the tracker spreadsheet at /JobSearch/tracker.xlsx with one row per company.
After updating, [flag rule] and mark them in a "Needs Follow-Up" column.
tokens: surface any thread silent for 14+ days

blocks.text: Walking the Chain
Great job! Codex now runs each stage and passes the result to the next.

• The "gather" pulls 23 emails.
  • The extract step turns those into 9 companies, each with a status.
  • The file step saves 11 PDFs into folders.
  • The "update" writes to the spreadsheet.
  • The flag step finds three threads that have been silent for over two weeks.
One brief in one chain gave five outputs. The workflow itself is built, but nothing is running on a schedule yet.
A Useful Toggle Before the First Run

When you run the chain for the first time, turn on Plan mode — a toggle next to the prompt bar. With it on, Codex writes out the steps it intends to take before executing: which emails it'll pull, which statuses it'll extract, where it'll save the PDFs, and which threads it'll flag. You read the plan, fix anything that's off, and only then does the chain run. After a few successful runs, you can turn it off and let Codex execute directly.

feedbackCorrect.text: A chain has more places to go wrong than a single task. Run it end-to-end on real data, check the output at each stage, and fix any issues. Once the manual run looks right, the schedule is safe.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Running it on the schedule first means you might not see a stage failure until a week later, and by then, several runs have already gone wrong. Test the full chain manually first; schedule only what you've verified works.

options.label: Test each stage in a separate chat first
Run it manually once on real data and check every stage's output
Set the schedule and trust the first run to surface any issues

blocks.question: Before you schedule this workflow, what should you do?

blocks.text: Turn the Tested Workflow Into a Skill
Great! The workflow now works, but its rules still live within a single task. You can change that. Ask Codex to turn the approved process into a reusable Skill:

“Create a Skill called job-search-update. Include the status rules, tracker columns, attachment rules, follow-up threshold, and every case that must be flagged for review.” Review the drafted Skill before saving it. To trigger the skill in the desktop app, use the "$" command.
Schedule the Skill

Now, it's time to build your automation. Stay in the tested Codex task and ask: “Every Friday at 5 p.m., return to this task and run $job-search-update. Use the Gmail plugin and the Job Search project. Do not send emails. Post a summary of changes and list anything that needs my decision.” Review the drafted task before confirming it. Because the workflow updates a local spreadsheet and folders, the computer must remain on, the ChatGPT desktop app must be running, and the project must be available at run time.
Friday Evening Arrives
Friday evening arrives. Your computer and the ChatGPT desktop app are running, but you don’t need to start the workflow yourself. Saturday morning, you check the project:

• The tracker has new rows for the three companies you applied to this week
  • Two folders of PDFs are filed
  • The "Needs Follow-Up" column shows two threads to chase on Monday.
The work that used to never happen is now done with no effort on your part.
Check It From Your Phone

You don't have to be at your computer to see what your automations did. Open Remote in the ChatGPT mobile app Settings to connect to Codex running on your computer. First, select Connections in the desktop app, then proceed with the linking process. Both devices must use the same ChatGPT account and workspace.
From your phone, you can:

• Start or continue tasks on the connected computer
  • Send instructions and answer Codex's questions
  • Approve actions
  • Review outputs, screenshots, terminal results, and file changes
  • Receive notifications when a task finishes or needs attention

  • Produce: Build a post-trip to-do list (expenses to submit, missing receipts, anything that needs follow-up).
What changes is the trigger — not a weekly schedule, but after each trip ends. And one stage hits a wall that plugins can't get past on their own.
The Receipt Behind the Login

Your hotel booking confirmation lives in Gmail — the plugin covers that. But the itemized receipt, the one with line items and taxes you need for records, is only on the booking site. This is where Computer Use earns its place. Codex can open the site, navigate to the trip, download the receipt, and save it to the project folder.

Keep Computer Use tasks narrow and review the apps and actions it requests. Close unrelated sensitive windows, and stay present whenever the workflow involves an account, login, payment, privacy setting, or other confidential information.

If a password or security check appears, complete it yourself before the workflow continues.
blocks.title: 💡 Stay Present for Sensitive Steps

blocks.text: Setting Up the Trip Project

Create a new Codex project — call it "Trips." Connect the same Gmail plugin (you already authorized it once, so the connection is quick), and add Computer Use for the hotel-portal step. Now it's time to write a new brief.

blocks.exampleResponse: Trip workflow ready. Run after each trip ends.
